Afghanistan.d:
Since the Taliban took Kabul in 2021, the factions running Afghanistan's ministries include some that foreign governments and the UN tie to outside armed powers. The clearest example is the Haqqani network, a militant group inside the Taliban that the top US military officer once called an arm of Pakistan's military intelligence service, the ISI: it was handed Kabul's security, and its leader became interior minister. Pakistan denies the tie. UN sanctions monitors, who report each year on the Taliban and al-Qaeda, find al-Qaeda-affiliated figures among senior Taliban officials and say parts of the government give strong support to the Pakistani Taliban, an armed group fighting Pakistan's state. The Taliban reject those reports.

Before 2021 the reach-in came mainly through money. Kabul Bank, which paid the wages of soldiers, police and civil servants, counted brothers of the president and the first vice-president among its shareholders and lent most of its deposits to a small circle of insiders; about $935 million was lost, the public rescue cost more than 5% of a year's economic output, and neither brother was charged.

For people living there, this means the police in the capital answer to a faction accused of serving a neighbouring country's spy service, and the government that should protect them gives room to armed groups the UN lists as terrorist. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Afghanistan 9 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and 1.5 out of 10 for the courts, police and watchdogs that could push back, so residents have almost nowhere to take a complaint.

Angola.d:
Angola's state runs mainly on oil, and the state oil company, Sonangol, is where foreign traders reach in. The clearest case came out in a Swiss court: Trafigura, one of the world's largest oil and metals traders, paid €4.3 million in 2009–11 to an Angolan official linked to a Sonangol subsidiary, and in January 2025 it and its former chief operating officer were convicted. Trafigura has appealed.

A second, quieter route runs through the networks that train future leaders. Vera Daves de Sousa, finance minister since October 2019, is listed among alumni of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme. The Forum is the Swiss organisation behind the yearly Davos meeting and works to bring companies and governments together on policy; its programme gives people under about 40 five years of meetings and courses. Being selected is not wrongdoing, but it ties the person who runs the country's money to a business-led network abroad.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Angola 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 4 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, this means the oil revenue that pays for schools, hospitals and wages has been a target for foreign companies willing to pay officials, and the checks that should catch those payments are weak at home.

Australia.d:
In Australia, outsiders reach in through three main routes: foreign governments buying access to politicians, drug importers buying officers at the border, and private firms and gangs getting people into the bodies that write rules or spend public money.

The foreign route is best documented for China's United Front, the Chinese Communist Party office that organises influence abroad through community and business groups. A property developer who chaired a council linked to it gave about AU$2 million to Labor and more than AU$1 million to the Liberal Party with associates, paid a senator's legal bills through a linked company, and had his residency cancelled on security-service advice. Community leaders tied to the same network have since been prosecuted under Australia's foreign-interference law, and India's foreign intelligence service has cultivated politicians and a state police force.

Lower down, drug importers have recruited Border Force and state police officers in Sydney and Melbourne, and courts in both states have convicted such officers repeatedly since 2016; Australia pays some of the world's highest wholesale drug prices, which is what makes an insider worth buying. In Victoria, members of outlaw motorcycle gangs held union posts on state-funded building sites until the federal government took over that union division in 2024. Inside government, a PwC partner hired by the Treasury to advise on laws against multinational tax avoidance passed its confidential plans to colleagues at a firm that advised the companies those laws targeted.

For people living there, this means the officers checking cargo may be paid by importers, public building money can pass through gang-linked hands, and tax laws meant to make large companies pay can be weakened before they are written.

Bahrain.d:
Nothing is documented yet of outside groups placing people or money inside Bahrain's government or companies, so this is an estimate based on conditions.

Bahrain is a small Gulf kingdom whose politics are shaped by the rivalry between Sunni-led Gulf states and Shia Iran. Two outside movements are relevant. The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement active across the Arab world, has a documented presence in Bahrain. Groups allied with Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the branch of Iran's armed forces that backs allied movements abroad, are thought to be present but are not documented. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Bahrain 4.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 5.3 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, both in the middle of the range.

For people living there, this means there is no named case to challenge, and the likeliest outside pressure is political and religious rather than criminal: movements backed by other states competing for influence over Bahrain's communities and its government. If that pressure reached inside the state, residents would see it first in who is appointed to security posts and religious bodies, and with no documented case, the cost to them is not known.

Belgium.d:
Belgium is where outsiders reach into Europe as a whole. Brussels hosts the main EU institutions and NATO, and Antwerp is the port through which more cocaine reaches Europe than any other, so foreign governments, companies and drug networks all have reasons to get people inside.

In Antwerp, cocaine networks pay port workers, terminal staff, customs officers and police to pull containers out and pass on access codes and information, and courts have convicted insiders from all of those groups in trial after trial since 2018. A 2025 EU review of European ports concluded that criminal networks had significantly penetrated them, because the loads being seized were too large to move without help from inside; Antwerp alone seized 116 tonnes of cocaine in 2023.

In Brussels the reach-in is political. Belgian prosecutors say Qatar and Morocco paid cash to members of the European Parliament, partly through a human-rights charity, to favour them, a case known as Qatargate in which a vice-president of the Parliament was removed and charged; the accused deny it. A separate probe alleges that associates of a Huawei lobbyist paid MEPs to oppose limits on Chinese 5G equipment. Foreign spy services also work from inside: China's, Hungary's and Morocco's intelligence services have each been found paying a Belgian politician, trying to recruit EU officials or placing their members on the staff of a mosque the state was asked to recognise.

For people living in Belgium and across the EU, this means decisions on trade, technology and human rights may have been shaped by foreign payments, and the officers checking cargo at Antwerp may be working for the networks they are meant to stop.

Bolivia.d:
Bolivia is one of the world's main producers of coca, the plant cocaine is made from, and the documented pattern here is traffickers buying the officers whose job is to stop them. Twice in recent years, a former head of Bolivia's anti-narcotics police force, the FELCN, has been convicted in the United States of working for traffickers: one agreed to protect cocaine loads bound for Miami, and the other, who led the force until 2019, steered investigations away from allied traffickers and assigned armed officers to guard their loads.

Outside parties have also reached the state at the top. After the 1980 'cocaine coup', so called because of the military government's ties to traffickers, journalist Robert Parry wrote that the Unification Church, the Korean-founded religious movement of Sun Myung Moon, and its political arm backed the new regime and that Moon's aide met the coup leader. That rests on one writer's account.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Bolivia 6.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 4.6 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, this means the police unit they would turn to about a trafficking gang has, at least twice, been run by someone on a gang's payroll, and investigations have been pointed away from favoured traffickers and towards their rivals. Both convictions came from US courts, which means Bolivians learned how their own anti-drug force was run from a foreign trial rather than from their own institutions.

Brunei.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Brunei, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign intelligence service, company, crime group, church or lodge paying or placing people inside its government.

Brunei is a small, oil-rich sultanate on Borneo where the sultan holds executive power and there is no elected parliament, so there are few public channels through which outside influence would come to light. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Brunei 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, low by world standards, and about 4.6 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs.

For people living there, this means there is no documented case of an official acting for an outside interest, and the low score suggests the risk is small. With few public channels and middling oversight, though, such a case would be hard to bring to light, and a documented case would change this estimate.

Cabo Verde.d:
Little is documented for Cabo Verde, so this is an estimate. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, criminal group or lodge paying or placing people inside its government. The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country low for officials working for criminal interests and comparatively strong in its courts, police and watchdogs, which suggests fewer officials act for outside interests here than in most of West Africa. The islands sit on Atlantic shipping lanes between South America, West Africa and Europe, so the ports are the place most exposed to outside money.

The lack of cases may also reflect how little investigative reporting covers the islands. If outside money does reach officials, it would most likely show up in the ports, in shipping and in public contracts, and residents would pay for it through lost public revenue rather than through anything they could see directly. For now there is no named official, company or group for Cabo Verdeans to hold to account.

Central African Republic.d:
In the Central African Republic a foreign armed group works from inside the state. Wagner, the Russian private military company tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, arrived in 2018 and placed its own people in the presidency: one of its men, Valery Zakharov, served as President Touadéra's national security adviser and was sanctioned by the United States for his Wagner ties. A US-sponsored research centre, the Africa Center for Strategic Studies, assesses that the old Wagner organisation has in effect taken over the state.

The arrangement has spread into the drug trade. Reporting from Bangui in 2026 describes Wagner's remnants supplying tramadol, an opioid painkiller, to members of the presidential guard and to a youth militia, with senior security officials alleged to control the market and payments flowing to Wagner and allied armed groups along the smuggling route. No one has been charged.

For people in the country, the president's security advice has come from a Wagner man answerable to Moscow rather than to Central African voters or courts, and some of the armed men around them are supplied with opioids by the same network. The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country among the very worst in the world for officials working for criminal interests, with almost no capacity in its courts, police or watchdogs to resist. Under the previous president, press reports said he had joined Freemasonry under the sponsorship of the Republic of Congo's president.

Colombia.d:
In Colombia the drug trade and the armed groups built on it have reached into every level of the state. The cocaine cartels and the AUC, right-wing paramilitaries who were also major traffickers, paid into presidential campaigns, bought the security officers around presidents and placed allies in Congress. In the 'parapolítica' scandal, about 30% of Congress was investigated, charged or convicted over collusion with the paramilitaries, and more than 500 elected officials were investigated over a decade. Some of those legislators then bought the court that tries them: in the 'Cartel de la Toga', two former Supreme Court presidents and the national anti-corruption prosecutor were convicted of taking money to bury cases.

The reach continues at local level today. Trafficking groups such as the Gulf Clan, the country's largest, fund mayoral candidates in the towns along their routes and have hidden their property in the names of people inside the justice system, in one case a serving prosecutor, so that their assets sit under official protection. Foreign construction companies have paid in as well, including into a presidential campaign.

For Colombians, this has meant voting for legislators and mayors whose campaigns traffickers helped fund, and taking cases before judges and prosecutors paid to bury files. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Colombia high for officials working for criminal interests, but its courts have shown they can reach their own members, which is how most of this became known. A Pentecostal church founded in Colombia also runs its own party, MIRA, which puts church members into the Senate and local councils.

Costa Rica.d:
Costa Rica lies on the route that carries Colombian cocaine north to the United States and across to Europe, and traffickers keep that route open by recruiting people inside the police and the security ministry to tell them what investigators know. The clearest case reaches near the top: the US Treasury found that a former vice-minister of public security, who later sat as a judge, helped move cocaine through the country and used his government contacts to learn about open drug investigations. He was arrested on a US extradition request in 2025, shortly after Costa Rica changed its constitution to allow its own citizens to be extradited for drug trafficking. He has not been convicted.

The same method works lower down. On the Caribbean side, where the cocaine corridor runs through the lowlands, trafficking groups have recruited local police officers to warn them of raids, checkpoints and investigators' movements, and several have been charged.

For people living along that corridor, the officers they would call for help may be the ones telling traffickers when the police are coming, and drug investigations may be known to the traffickers before they reach court. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Costa Rica's officials as relatively unlikely to work for criminal interests, with institutions of middling strength.

Cyprus.d:
No case on the map currently shows a foreign state, company, criminal group or lodge placing people inside the Cypriot government or paying its officials to act for it. Cyprus is a small European Union member with a large financial and company-registration sector serving foreign clients, which is where outside money would most likely touch officials: through bank supervision, company registration and residence decisions.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cyprus low to middling for officials working for criminal interests, but its courts, police and watchdogs score weak for an EU member. That means that if outside money did reach officials, the institutions meant to detect it are weaker than in most of the bloc.

For residents, the absence of a documented case here is not proof that none exists. It means that the cases on record do not show outside interests deciding public matters in Cyprus, and that there is no named official, company or group on the map for Cypriots to hold to account.

Dominica.d:
The one documented case of outside money reaching Dominica's government involves a campaign donation. Al Jazeera reported that an Iranian businessman gave hundreds of thousands of dollars to Prime Minister Roosevelt Skerrit's election campaign and received an ambassador's post and a diplomatic passport in return; the businessman was later jailed in Iran for stealing oil revenue. Skerrit denies any trade, and no court has ruled on the claim.

If the report is right, a post that speaks for Dominica abroad went to a campaign donor, and a diplomatic passport, which carries legal protections overseas, went to a man later jailed for theft. Dominicans have no public record of what campaign donors receive.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Dominica low for officials working for criminal interests, with institutions of middling strength.

El Salvador.d:
El Salvador's two largest gangs, MS-13 and Barrio 18, grew out of Salvadoran communities in Los Angeles and now run neighbourhoods across the country. According to the US government, officials of President Nayib Bukele's administration negotiated with the gangs' leaders from inside the prison system. The US Treasury says the prisons director and the head of a government programme for violence-hit neighbourhoods gave gang leaders money and privileges in prison. In return, the gangs were to keep the number of killings down and support the government at elections. A US indictment of 13 MS-13 leaders adds that the meetings were organised by the government and prison officials, that one leader wanted in the United States was released, and that the gang backed Bukele's party, Nuevas Ideas, in the 2021 election. El Faro, a Salvadoran news site, first reported the talks in 2020. The government denies any pact, and no court has tried the claims.

If the US account is right, a criminal organisation bargained directly with the state over how many Salvadorans would be killed and how people would vote. Salvadorans cannot check how much of the fall in killings came from such a deal, because the evidence has never been heard by a court at home. Voters in 2021 did not know of the alleged gang support for the governing party. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10 and the strength of courts and watchdogs at 3.25.

Eswatini.d:
This is an estimate: no case on the map shows a foreign state, company, criminal group or religious body placing or paying people inside Eswatini's government. Eswatini is a small kingdom between South Africa and Mozambique where the king holds executive power and political parties cannot compete for government, so there are few independent sources inside the country that report on officials.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 6.5 out of 10, in its high band, and the courts, police and watchdogs that would resist them at about 3.2. A country with that profile, on the trade routes between South Africa and Mozambique, is one where traffickers and businesses seeking contracts would find officials open to payment and little chance of a case reaching court.

If that is happening, people in Eswatini would pay for it through public contracts that cost more than they should and policing that does not reach those who pay. With no named case, there is no official, company or group they can point to or hold to account.

France.d:
In France the outside interests that reach into government mostly come in through the people who run it, not through bribes paid to officials. The clearest channel is the move from private banking into the offices that set economic policy. Two French presidents worked at the Rothschild investment bank before entering government, among them the current one, Emmanuel Macron, a partner there until he joined the president's office in 2012. No court or inquiry has found that the bank directed policy, and the claim that the Rothschild family runs France is an antisemitic conspiracy theory. Private networks also pick future leaders early: the World Economic Forum, the Swiss foundation behind the Davos meeting, chose two of the last three presidents for its leadership network when they were young politicians.

Companies also work through ministers once they are in office; leaked internal Uber documents show Macron, as economy minister, helping the US ride-hailing company against his own cabinet colleagues. Freemasonry, a society of private lodges whose members pledge mutual help, has long had members in French cabinets and senior posts, and the government itself now says the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist movement founded in Egypt, is working its way into local councils from the bottom up.

For people in France, this means decisions about banking, taxis or local services may already have been shaped by a firm or network before ministers present them, and the public sees the result without the contacts that produced it. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 3.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at just over 7, so outright bribery of officials is rare, and the influence that matters comes through who holds office.

Germany.d:
Germany is a target for foreign intelligence services because of its weight in the European Union and its industry, and they work by recruiting people close to power rather than paying officials outright. The spy services of Russia, China and Egypt have each had someone of their own working inside German institutions in recent years: in the top management of a payments company listed among Germany's largest firms, in the office of a member of the European Parliament, and in the government press office. Foreign governments also use money; German prosecutors have investigated several MPs for taking payments from Azerbaijan or from a Russian-funded network to speak for those countries in parliament and in the Council of Europe.

Companies and banks reach in through people and paperwork. Recent leaders of German financial policy have come from large US finance firms: Chancellor Friedrich Merz chaired the German arm of BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, until 2020, and a recent finance minister spent 17 years at Goldman Sachs. A study for MEPs found that Germany's risk agency copied large parts of the glyphosate makers' own application into the safety review the EU used to renew the weedkiller. At Hamburg and Bremerhaven, Germany's main container ports, cocaine importers recruit customs officers and terminal staff to clear containers.

For people in Germany, this means critics of Moscow and Beijing live alongside people those governments have recruited inside parliament and business, and a safety decision about a chemical used on farms and gardens rested partly on text the makers wrote. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 2 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at over 7, so most of these cases are investigated and some reach court.

Guatemala.d:
Guatemala lies on the land route that carries South American cocaine north to Mexico and the United States, and the trafficking groups that use it buy officials at every level the drugs pass through. Since 2005 the people charged, convicted or sanctioned in the United States for working with traffickers have included the head of Guatemala's anti-narcotics police and his deputy, town mayors along the Mexican border and the Pacific coast, a member of Congress, a member of the Central American Parliament, and a vice-president and interior minister. Some trafficking groups put their own people into office: the US Treasury says the Los Pochos group was run by a serving mayor and that its members still take part in local politics.

Corruption inside the state runs on the same lines. A customs bribery ring known as La Línea reached the president and vice-president, who were forced from office and later jailed. It was exposed by Guatemalan prosecutors with the help of CICIG, a UN-backed commission set up to take apart criminal networks inside the state, which the government later shut down.

For Guatemalans this means the police officer, mayor or legislator they would turn to may be working for traffickers, and import duties that should reach the treasury have gone to officials instead. Most cases against powerful figures are now heard in US courts rather than at home. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at 4.

Haiti.d:
In Haiti armed gangs control much of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and large areas of the Artibonite valley, and the line between the gangs and the state has worn thin from both sides. Politicians have funded and armed gangs to control territory and voters: Canada and the United States have sanctioned a former president, sitting and former senators and other political figures for financing gangs, and a UN panel of experts says former legislators have armed groups and used them to drive violence before elections. Those named deny it, and none has been tried.

The gangs in turn reach into the state. The UN panel reported in October 2026 that some police officers supply gangs with weapons and information, and that at least one member of the new municipal commission in Cité Soleil, one of the capital's poorest districts, is an active gang member. Cocaine traffickers have used Haiti as a stop on the route to the United States, and the US Treasury says the former president Michel Martelly worked with them and sponsored gangs; he denies it. Senior police have taken traffickers' money before: a former police commander admitted taking millions in bribes to protect cocaine shipments.

For people in Haiti, this means the gangs that kill, kidnap and drive them from their homes are paid for by some of the politicians asking for their votes and supplied by some of the police meant to protect them. With courts and watchdogs scoring 2.2 out of 10 on the Global Organized Crime Index and officials acting for criminal interests at 8.5, none of the sanctioned politicians has faced a Haitian court.

India.d:
India's government is run largely by members of one organisation. The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) is a Hindu nationalist volunteer body founded in 1925; it trains full-time organisers and lends them to the governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which grew out of its political wing. Prime Minister Narendra Modi was one of those organisers before the RSS assigned him to the party. By the press's count, about seven in ten BJP ministers have RSS roots, including those who set economic policy, and so does the vice president who chairs the upper house. Membership is lawful, but the RSS publishes no list, so voters learn who belongs only from biographies and newspaper tallies.

Crime and money reach the state by other routes. Nearly half the MPs elected in 2024, 251 of 543, declared pending criminal cases, and in states such as Uttar Pradesh gang leaders have held seats for years, sometimes while in prison. Large companies that depend on state contracts for ports, power and airports are accused of paying officials for them; US prosecutors charge that the Adani Group paid more than $250 million in bribes for solar power contracts, which Adani denies.

For people in India this means their laws are drafted by a cabinet drawn mostly from an organisation they cannot see into, and passed by a parliament in which nearly half the members face criminal charges. When a public contract is suspected of having been bought, the question is often first tested in a foreign court rather than an Indian one.

Ireland.d:
In the decades after independence, a Catholic men's order had members at the top of Irish government. The Knights of Saint Columbanus, founded in 1915 and long described as secretive, counted the Taoiseach of the first Inter-Party government from 1948, John A. Costello, and other members of his cabinet among its members, according to biographers. Knights also sat in the civil service, and the order's governing council reportedly received assurances from a justice minister that the government would avoid conflict between Church and State. A Labour Knight is reported to have worked against a plan for free state care of mothers and children that the Catholic archbishop of Dublin opposed.

Today the visible links run through private international forums of business and political leaders. The World Economic Forum, a Geneva-based foundation funded by large companies, has enrolled recent Irish leaders in its Young Global Leaders network while they were in office, among them Taoiseach Leo Varadkar. Membership is lawful and no finding shows these forums directed a decision.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Ireland 4 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and above 7 for its courts and watchdogs. For people in Ireland this means their leaders meet business and political figures in settings where no public record is kept, and that past decisions on their families' health care were shaped in part by an order whose meetings were also private.

Japan.d:
In Japan, religious movements and nationalist lobbies have built ties with the governing Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) by supplying what a campaign needs: organised votes, volunteers, event audiences and money. The Unification Church, a Korean-founded movement, is the best recorded. After the 2022 killing of former prime minister Shinzo Abe, the LDP's own survey found that 179 of its 379 members of parliament had ties to the church, some of them using its followers as campaign workers. Tokyo courts have since ordered the church's Japanese branch dissolved for pressuring followers into ruinous donations. Komeito, the party of the Buddhist lay movement Soka Gakkai, governed alongside the LDP for most of 1999 to 2025.

Nationalist lobbies sit closer still. Nippon Kaigi, a lobby that wants to rewrite the post-war constitution and school teaching, and the political arm of Japan's Shinto shrines each run a league of members of parliament, and press counts of those leagues have found a majority of cabinet ministers in one or both under recent prime ministers, including Sanae Takaichi, who belongs to Nippon Kaigi's league.

Industry has reached in by another route. A parliamentary inquiry into the 2011 Fukushima meltdown found that the nuclear regulator had come to serve the power companies it was meant to police. For voters in Japan, this means the people they elect may owe their campaigns to a church a court has ordered dissolved, and the ministers who shape their constitution and schools belong to lobbies whose membership the government does not disclose.

Kiribati.d:
No case on this map documents a foreign state, criminal group or company paying or placing officials inside Kiribati's government, so this account rests on general conditions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kiribati low, 1.5 out of 10, for officials working for criminal interests, but below 5 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. A weak oversight score means there are few institutions in a position to notice outside influence if it came.

For people in Kiribati this means the risk that officials are serving criminal interests appears low, but the means of checking are thin. If outside influence did reach their government, it would most likely show in fishing licences, aid-funded contracts or policing, and with limited courts and press it could go unexamined.

Kuwait.d:
In Kuwait the documented outside influence on government comes through an Islamist movement that works openly inside the constitution. The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt that aims to bring its members into power, has a Kuwaiti branch that broke with the international organisation after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990. It then formed its own party, the Islamic Constitutional Movement, known as Hadas, which regularly won several seats in parliament through the 1990s and 2000s and at times sent members into the cabinet, where they helped set policy. When its coalition boycotted the 2013 elections, it left parliament for that term.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kuwait 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and just over 5 for its courts and watchdogs. For Kuwaitis this means a Brotherhood-derived party, banned in neighbouring Saudi Arabia, has been one of the parties they can vote for and has had a hand in government, and that when it boycotts, its voters go unrepresented. Beyond that, residents face the moderate level of corruption and organised crime the index measures, which no documented case yet maps.

Lebanon.d:
In Lebanon, an armed party aligned with Iran sits inside the government. Hezbollah, a Shia party with its own armed wing, holds about 14 of the 128 seats in parliament, and in the government formed in 2025 its nominees run the health and labour ministries; with its ally Amal it controls six of the 24 portfolios. At least 28 countries, including the US and the UK, list it as a terrorist organisation, and in 2019 the US sanctioned two of its sitting MPs, along with the official who handles Hezbollah's dealings with Lebanon's police and army. The cabinet has set the goal that only the state should hold weapons, and Hezbollah's leader has rejected the army's plan to disarm it.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Lebanon 9.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs, close to the worst results in the world. For people in Lebanon this means a party with its own army, aligned with a foreign state, sits in the cabinet that is supposed to decide when the country goes to war. While that party keeps its own weapons, the Lebanese state does not decide alone whether the country fights.

Liechtenstein.d:
No case has been recorded of a foreign government, crime group or company paying Liechtenstein's officials or placing its own people inside the principality's government, courts or firms, so what follows is an estimate drawn from general conditions rather than from documented events.

The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country, places Liechtenstein among the countries where officials are least likely to work for criminal or outside interests, and rates its courts, police and watchdogs as strong.

For people who live in Liechtenstein, those conditions suggest that officials rarely act for someone else's interests and that a complaint about it would be heard. If that changes, residents would most likely learn of it the way people in neighbouring countries have: through a court case, a regulator's ruling or a published investigation.

Malawi.d:
In Malawi, the documented outside reach is through the procurement of the country's security forces, where a single foreign supplier is alleged to have bought his way into contracts with the police and the army. Malawi's anti-corruption bureau reported in 2022 that companies linked to Zuneth Sattar, a UK-based businessman, won contracts worth more than 150 million dollars from both forces over four years, and that he paid officials to secure them. The bureau's report named dozens of people, and arrests reached a former police chief, a cabinet minister and the vice president, who denied wrongdoing and died in a plane crash in 2024. These are findings and arrests, not convictions.

The mechanism is common where security spending is large and kept away from public scrutiny: the buyer is the state, the details are confidential on security grounds, and one well-connected supplier can win repeated contracts if the officials signing them are paid. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Malawi's institutions as weak and finds a moderate level of officials serving outside interests.

For Malawians this means that tax money meant to equip the police and army went, through contracts the bureau says were bought, to the companies of one outside supplier, with the alleged payments reaching as far as the vice president's office. The cases have not been decided, so people still do not know who in their government took part or what the public received for the money.

Malta.d:
In Malta, outside interests have reached the state in two ways: through private companies that win large state contracts with help from the people closest to the prime minister, and through the licences Malta grants to firms that then operate across the European Union.

The clearest example of the first is the gas power station built under a state contract. One of the builder's directors secretly owned a company in Dubai that leaked papers listed as expected to pay into secret Panama companies set up for the energy minister and the prime minister's chief of staff; the journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was investigating that company when a car bomb killed her in 2017, and the director now faces trial over her murder while all three men face corruption charges. A public inquiry found that the Maltese state had created an 'atmosphere of impunity'.

The second channel runs through Malta's online gambling industry. Because a Maltese licence lets a betting firm operate across the EU, Italian mafia groups, including the 'Ndrangheta from Calabria and Cosa Nostra from Sicily, have secretly owned or run Malta-licensed betting companies to collect bets and launder money, according to Italian investigations over the past decade. Malta's regulator suspended licences once the investigations surfaced.

For people in Malta this means they pay for electricity from a plant whose contract prosecutors say was tied to payments meant for the two men around the prime minister, and the reporter who tried to expose it was killed. It also means their country's licences have served as cover for mafias, and the Global Organized Crime Index finds officials there often serving criminal or outside interests.

Mexico.d:
In Mexico, drug cartels put officials on their payroll at every level of government, from town police to the federal cabinet. Cartels are large trafficking organisations such as the Sinaloa Cartel and the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG). Where a cartel controls a route or a town, it pays the local police to work for it, buys the state prosecutor and security chief who decide which cases go forward, and in several states has reached the governor. US and Mexican courts and the US government have acted against cartel-paid officials ranging from mayors and judges to state governors and a federal security minister, and whole municipal police forces in Michoacán, Guerrero, Tamaulipas and elsewhere have been disbanded or taken over by federal forces because they worked for cartels. The clearest example is Iguala in 2014, where the mayor and town police acted for a local gang and police took 43 students who then disappeared.

Foreign companies seeking business have paid officials at Pemex, the state oil company. Writers have also claimed that El Yunque, a secret Catholic group, placed members in the governing PAN party and in a president's cabinet; the PAN denies it.

For Mexicans this means the police officer, prosecutor or governor they depend on may be working for the people they should be stopping, and a crime reported to them may go straight to the cartel. Many of these cases are tried only in the United States. When the US charged a former defence minister in 2020, it dropped the case after Mexico objected, and Mexico's own inquiry closed without charges.

Mongolia.d:
Nothing is documented of a foreign state, company, crime group or religious body paying or placing people inside Mongolia's government, so this is an estimate based on conditions.

Mongolia sits between Russia and China, its two large neighbours and main trading routes. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a moderate level of officials serving criminal or outside interests and rates its courts, police and watchdogs in the middle range. A country with that profile is one where outside money could reach some officials, most likely through licences and public contracts, but where institutions have some capacity to notice and respond.

For people in Mongolia this means there is no named official, company or group acting for an outside interest that they can point to or hold to account. The estimate rests on the index's assessment rather than on any inquiry or court ruling, and a documented case would change it.

Myanmar.d:
In Myanmar the army has drawn armed crime groups into the state itself, and those groups run drug production and scam centres along the borders with China and Thailand. Militias that the army has formally placed under its command, and armed groups allied with it, control the areas of Shan and Karen states that produce much of Asia's methamphetamine and host compounds where trafficked workers are held and forced to defraud strangers online. Their leaders hold military rank, seats in parliament and state honours, while partnering with Chinese-run crime groups that build and run the scam centres. The clearest example is the Karen Border Guard Force, a militia under the army whose commander partnered in building the scam city of Shwe Kokko and received a top state honour from the junta; the UK and US have since sanctioned him over forced labour.

A Buddhist nationalist monks' group, Ma Ba Tha, reached into lawmaking. The religious affairs ministry drafted four 'race and religion' laws from texts its members proposed, and parliament passed them in 2015. They restrict religious conversion and marriage between Buddhist women and non-Buddhist men.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds Myanmar's officials serving criminal interests to one of the highest degrees in the world, with almost no court or police capacity to check them. For people in Shan and Karen states this means living beside drug labs and guarded compounds run by forces the army counts as its own. Muslim residents and Buddhist women live under marriage and conversion rules drawn from a monks' movement's drafts.

Netherlands.d:
In the Netherlands, the clearest reach into institutions comes from cocaine gangs working through the people who run the country's ports and courts, while large companies reach into government policy.

Rotterdam is Europe's largest port, and gangs importing cocaine recruit terminal workers and IT contractors who can hand over the PIN codes that release a container, or change where boxes are stacked, so that extraction crews can pull out the drugs before customs checks. Dutch and Belgian courts have convicted such insiders many times in recent years. The same gangs reach into the justice system: the network of Ridouan Taghi got a police employee and lawyers to work for it, one of them carrying his messages out of a maximum-security prison, and during his trial a witness's brother and the witness's lawyer were murdered.

Two of the country's largest multinationals lobbied coalition talks into planning a tax cut for shareholders that no party had campaigned for. The king and a defence minister are listed in the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders network.

For people in the Netherlands this means violence near the ports and around trials, as gangs that have bought insiders protect their trade.

Nigeria.d:
In Nigeria the people reaching into government are mostly after oil. Foreign oil companies and commodity traders have paid officials for licences, cargoes and favourable legal outcomes, and several have admitted it, or been found to have done it, in foreign courts. A US diplomatic cable records a Shell executive saying in 2009 that the company had seconded its own staff to every ministry dealing with oil, which Shell denies.

The cost falls on the public treasury: money lost to a bribed contract, an oil block sold through a former minister's company, or an arbitration award obtained by fraud is money that does not reach schools, clinics or roads. In one dispute a London judge found that a company had bribed a government lawyer to win an award that would have left Nigeria owing over $11 billion.

Pressure also comes from inside the country. Confraternities, secretive brotherhoods that began at universities, are hired by politicians for election work, and some have been rewarded with government posts; police in several countries treat the best known of them, Black Axe, as an organised crime group, even though Nigeria's constitution bars members of secret societies from elected office. Voters in states where this happens face intimidation at the polls, and senior police drug officers have been charged with trading the drugs they seized. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Nigeria high for officials working for criminal interests, with middling strength in its courts and watchdogs.

Pakistan.d:
In Pakistan, outside forces reach into the state through two channels: international lenders at the moment of a bailout, and religious movements that turn devotion into votes or recruit inside the army.

The lender channel runs through the economic offices that a bailout depends on. The International Monetary Fund lends to countries in crisis on condition that they change policy, and during the 2019 talks an IMF staff member was made governor of the central bank, the official who sets interest rates and manages the currency. For three years the person deciding what Pakistanis paid to borrow and what their rupee was worth came from the lender's own staff.

Religious movements work from two directions. Families with hereditary custody of Sufi shrines draw income and votes from devotees and turn them into seats and ministries, so voters in shrine areas may back a family out of religious duty rather than on policy. Hizb ut-Tahrir, a banned international movement that seeks a single Islamic state, has recruited serving officers, and army officers up to the rank of brigadier have been convicted of links to it after the army said the group was working towards a coup.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Pakistan high for officials working for criminal interests and low for the strength of its courts and police.

Paraguay.d:
Paraguay's record shows criminal and foreign-linked money reaching both the top of government and the middle of the justice system. The Global Organized Crime Index gives it one of the highest scores in the world for officials working for criminal interests.

At the top, the reach runs through the Tri-Border Area around Ciudad del Este, where free-zone trade lets goods and money move with little checking and where Hezbollah, the Lebanese armed movement and party, has long had finance networks. The US Treasury sanctioned a former president and a sitting vice-president in 2023, saying their representatives collected bribes at private Hezbollah events in Paraguay; the sanctions on the former president were lifted in 2025 without any court ruling either way, so Paraguayans were left with an accusation against him that was neither tested nor withdrawn.

In the middle, cocaine networks shipping along the Hidrovía, the river route from Paraguay to the Atlantic, keep police officers, prosecutors, court staff and legislators on their side, so that cargo moves and cases stall. The clearest example is a 2022 investigation that charged all of these, including a sitting member of the Chamber of Deputies, while the network's central figure fled before arrest and one of the case's own prosecutors was removed.

For people in Paraguay this means the police who should investigate traffickers, the prosecutors who should charge them and the courts that should try them have all had members on the traffickers' side, and a dispute that reaches court may be heard by a system the network has already reached into.

Portugal.d:
In Portugal the documented pattern is a banking family that stayed close to government from the dictatorship onward, and whose money prosecutors say reached a prime minister.

Banco Espírito Santo, run by the Espírito Santo family, had been close to power since the Salazar dictatorship, and its last head was nicknamed 'owner of all this'. Its collapse in 2014 wiped out the savings and shares of people who had trusted it. Prosecutors say money from the group reached a former prime minister, José Sócrates, while he was in office; the trial began in 2025 and all defendants are presumed innocent. Portuguese voters are still waiting to learn whether a prime minister they elected was being paid by the country's most politically connected bank.

Outside that case, the record shows little organised crime inside Portuguese offices. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Portugal in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests and fairly well for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs.

International forums also reach Portuguese leaders: the World Economic Forum picked a future prime minister and European Commission president for its leadership network while he was foreign minister, though selection is not a finding of influence.

Rwanda.d:
In Rwanda the documented outside presence inside government is not hidden: a foreign-funded institute places its own advisers in the offices that plan and track what the state does. The Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, a London-based non-profit founded by the former UK prime minister, has supported units in the offices of the president and prime minister that set government priorities and check whether ministries deliver them, and has worked on Rwanda's system of performance contracts for officials. The institute reports work with governments in more than 45 countries, and its largest donor is the foundation of the American billionaire Larry Ellison.

The advisers are employed by the institute, not by the Rwandan state, and answer to their employer in London rather than to anyone Rwandans elect. Residents can read the programme descriptions the institute chooses to publish, but have no public way to see what advice was given or how its donors' priorities shaped it.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Rwanda in the middle range both for officials working for criminal or outside interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs.

Saudi Arabia.d:
In Saudi Arabia, the documented reach mostly runs outward: the state uses its money and its intelligence service to buy influence abroad.

Saudi intelligence and Saudi money have gone into foreign banks and alliances. The clearest example is Kamal Adham, head of Saudi intelligence until 1979, who fronted the secret takeover of a Washington bank by BCCI, a bank later closed worldwide for fraud, and paid a $105 million fine in the United States.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives Saudi Arabia one of the highest scores in the world for officials working for criminal interests, and residents have little way to check how state money spent abroad is used.

Sierra Leone.d:
Sierra Leone sits on the route that carries South American cocaine to Europe through West Africa, and traffickers using it look for protection inside the state rather than ways around it. They need the people who control an airport, an immigration desk or a landing clearance, and the record here shows them reaching each of those, up to the cabinet and, by press reports, the president's own family.

In 2008 a plane carrying about 700 kilograms of cocaine and painted with Red Cross markings landed at Lungi, the international airport, with help from airport and security staff who were later convicted; proceedings indicated that the aviation minister had cleared the landing, and he was dismissed but never tried. In 2025 Reuters reported that a Dutch cocaine trafficker on Europe's most-wanted lists had 'high-level protection' in the country and was married to the president's daughter; the government said it was investigating, dismissed the head of immigration, and denies knowing where he is.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 4. For people in Sierra Leone that means the convictions have reached baggage handlers and guards while the allegations against ministers and the presidential household stay untried, and police and immigration officers have little reason to act against a man said to be protected by the people they answer to.

Solomon Islands.d:
In the Solomon Islands foreign governments compete for the loyalty of members of parliament, and the money goes to MPs directly. Taiwan used to pay into a discretionary fund run by the prime minister's office, from which payments go to MPs, and when the country switched recognition from Taiwan to China in 2019, MPs told reporters that both Beijing and Taipei had offered them hundreds of thousands of dollars for their votes. China then took over the fund. In 2022 the prime minister's secretary told a parliamentary committee that Chinese money had gone to 39 of the 50 MPs in late 2021, weeks before Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare survived a no-confidence vote; the opposition said the money kept him in office, which his office denied.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7.5 out of 10. For voters this means they cannot tell whether their MP's vote was cast for them or for the government paying into the fund.

Spain.d:
Spain has two kinds of reach into its institutions, one from the drug trade along its coasts and one from a Catholic organisation into its government and banking.

Along the Strait of Gibraltar, eight miles from Morocco, drug networks recruit the officials who inspect what comes in. Around the port of Algeciras, Spain's largest container port, hashish and cocaine groups have paid municipal police, customs officers and dockworkers to wave loads through, and police operations keep arresting serving officers alongside the smugglers. The same groups recruit airport ground staff.

Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation of priests and lay members, reached the top of the state under the dictator Francisco Franco. From 1957 its members ran the finance, trade and planning ministries and opened Spain's closed economy, and by 1969 eleven members of Franco's cabinet had ties to it. Its members also formed the core shareholder group of Banco Popular, once Spain's sixth-largest bank, which a 2024 book says channelled money to Opus Dei causes; Opus Dei calls this false.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 5.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 6.7. For people around Algeciras it means living beside police officers and port staff who may be on a trafficker's payroll; for Banco Popular's shareholders, it meant losing everything when the bank was sold for one euro in 2017.

St. Vincent and the Grenadines.d:
Nothing is documented here, so this is an estimate. No case has been found of foreign governments, companies or criminal groups paying or placing officials in St Vincent and the Grenadines.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 2 out of 10, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5.4, near the middle of the scale. The pressure that exists nearby is the cocaine route north from South America through the eastern Caribbean.

For residents, this means there is no known case of an official here acting for an outside paymaster, and the low score suggests the risk is small. The estimate rests on the index's assessment rather than on any inquiry or court ruling in the country, so it describes what conditions suggest, not what has been checked, and a case that has not yet come to light would change it.

Switzerland.d:
Switzerland is where much of the world's governance sits, and much of the infiltration recorded here is aimed at those bodies rather than at the Swiss state. Geneva hosts the World Health Organization and the UN Human Rights Council, Zurich hosts FIFA and Basel the Bank for International Settlements, and outsiders have worked to get inside each. Tobacco companies spent years working through consultants and other UN agencies to weaken the WHO's tobacco work, according to a WHO expert inquiry. Private funders pay for WHO programmes they choose. Bid committees have allegedly paid FIFA and Olympic voters for hosting rights.

The country's banks and commodity traders are also a channel for reaching other governments. Swiss-based traders have been convicted of bribing officials who hand out oil contracts in Africa and Latin America.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 1.5 out of 10. For Swiss residents, it means paying for prosecutors who keep finding the country's banks and traders moving bribes, while decisions made in Geneva, Zurich and Basel shape health spending and bank lending in other countries.

Tanzania.d:
No case on the map documents outsiders paying or placing officials in Tanzania, but two patterns show where outside influence and the drug trade come close to the state.

The first is training. Since 2022 the Mwalimu Julius Nyerere Leadership School in Kibaha has taught officials from six southern African ruling parties, Tanzania's CCM among them along with South Africa's ANC and Zimbabwe's ZANU-PF. It was paid for with a $40 million grant from the Chinese Communist Party's Central Party School, and Chinese party theorists teach there. This is open, agreed by the governments involved, and gives a foreign ruling party a place to teach its methods to the people who run these states.

The second is drug money near the police. In 2017 the Dar es Salaam regional commissioner publicly named suspects in a drug-trafficking syndicate and ordered arrests that included 17 police officers. The naming was an accusation by an official, not a court finding.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 6 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 4.2. For Tanzanians, this means the people who run their ruling party are being taught by a foreign party under terms the public has not seen, and residents who were publicly named as traffickers carry the accusation without a court ever deciding it.

Tonga.d:
No case is documented of a foreign state, company or criminal group paying or placing officials inside Tonga's government, so this is an estimate based on conditions.

Tonga is a small kingdom where, until reforms in 2008, the monarch held most day-to-day power, and decisions about the country's money could be made by the king and a few advisers. The Global Organized Crime Index places Tonga in its Moderate band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 6 out of 10. That score suggests outside money could reach some officials, most likely through public contracts, licences or decisions made by a small circle around the government.

For people in Tonga this means there is no named official, company or group acting for an outside interest that they can point to or hold to account. The estimate rests on the index's assessment rather than on any inquiry or court ruling, and a documented case would change it.

Turkmenistan.d:
Turkmenistan is one of the most closed states on Earth: there is no independent press, no opposition party and no court that rules against the government. Almost nothing about how the state works is made public.

No case is documented of a foreign state, company or criminal group placing people inside the Turkmen government. The Global Organized Crime Index nonetheless puts Turkmenistan in its Severe band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 9 out of 10, among the highest scores in the world, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 2.2, among the lowest. No journalist, opposition party or independent court can check those officials, which is part of what the scores measure.

For people in Turkmenistan this means there is no journalist, judge or auditor in the country who can find out whether officials act for outside interests, and no public record that would show it if they did.

United Arab Emirates.d:
The United Arab Emirates uses its wealth to place its own people at the head of international bodies and to bring foreign institutions into its orbit. It gave Interpol's foundation about $54 million, reported to equal the regular dues of all other member countries combined, and in 2021 a senior UAE interior ministry official was elected Interpol's president despite complaints from detainees that he was responsible for their torture. In 2023 the chief executive of ADNOC, the state oil company, presided over the UN's COP28 climate talks, and leaked briefing papers showed his team preparing to raise oil and gas business in meetings with foreign governments.

The UAE is also a place where outside crime reaches others' governments. Dubai's free-zone companies, whose owners can stay hidden behind a required local sponsor, have been used by foreign drug organisations to employ the men who work for them, including one that prosecutors say paid politicians and a security chief in Bosnia.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in the UAE at 6.5 out of 10. For residents and visitors, this means the officials responsible for policing and detention in the UAE have also run the world's police cooperation body, so a complaint against them can reach the institution they lead.

Uzbekistan.d:
In Uzbekistan, foreign companies entered one of the country's most valuable markets by paying the president's family. Three foreign telecom groups, VimpelCom, Telia and MTS, paid companies controlled by Gulnara Karimova, elder daughter of then-President Islam Karimov, to obtain mobile licences and radio frequencies; Uzbek prosecutors put her kickbacks at $869 million, and the three firms later paid about $2.6 billion between them to settle foreign bribery cases. Karimova has been convicted twice in Uzbekistan and remains in prison.

The pattern shows how access to a closed economy worked: under Karimov, a foreign investor did not compete in an open tender but paid a gatekeeper close to the ruler. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Uzbekistan at 7 out of 10 and the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs at 3.8, so the conditions that made such deals possible have not gone away.

For people in Uzbekistan, this meant paying for a mobile service whose licences were sold privately to the president's daughter instead of to the operator offering the best terms. Most of the settlement money went to the governments of the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden, not to Uzbekistan, and weak courts leave citizens with little means to find out whether officials are making similar arrangements today.

Vietnam.d:
In Vietnam, the documented pattern is drug trafficking networks buying protection from the police officers assigned to stop them. Drugs reach Vietnam across its long border with Laos. Officers on drug investigation teams have been charged with shielding a Laos–Vietnam network that moved 137 kilograms of drugs, and a senior officer in Viet Tri was sentenced to life for buying a large consignment of tablets so he could stage an arrest and claim credit.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Vietnam in its High band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 7 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 4.8.

For people in Vietnam this matters because the country imposes the death penalty for trafficking amounts like those the officers handled. An ordinary courier caught with such a quantity can be executed, while the police who protected the network, or who bought the drugs themselves, are tried in the same courts. Residents who report drug dealing cannot be sure the officers they report it to are not on the network's side.

Albania.d:
Albania sits on one of the main routes by which cannabis and other drugs move from the Balkans across the Adriatic into Italy and the rest of the EU, and the trafficking groups on that route often work across both countries. The risk this creates is that family and political ties reach from those groups into the police and the ministries meant to stop the trade.

The clearest illustration reached the top of the police. Italian police arrested a cousin of the interior minister, the minister in charge of Albania's police, in a probe into an Albanian-Italian group moving cannabis, and wiretaps in that probe mentioned the minister. He was later convicted only of abuse of office; the trafficking charges did not end in a conviction, so no court has said whether the group had the minister working for it.

Albania is a candidate to join the EU, and how its courts handle ties between ministers and crime groups is one of the tests it is judged on. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Albania 6.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 5 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, the middle of the range. For people living there, this means the officials who decide which smuggling cases are pursued may be related to, or answerable to, the smugglers, and a verdict that leaves the trafficking question open does not tell them which it is.

Antigua and Barbuda.d:
Antigua and Barbuda earns money as an offshore financial centre, where foreign-run banks take deposits from around the world under Antiguan licences. The risk in that model is that a large foreign bank becomes more powerful than the small local body meant to supervise it, and the documented case here is exactly that: the bank bought its supervisor.

R. Allen Stanford ran Stanford International Bank from Antigua and was later convicted in the United States of a $7 billion fraud. The head of Antigua's financial regulator, the body that was supposed to check Stanford's bank, admitted in a US court that Stanford had paid him in cash, private-jet flights and sports tickets. In return he left the bank's real assets unexamined and turned away the US securities regulator by claiming his office had no power to help, when it did. He was extradited and jailed.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores the country 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 4.7 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, and for depositors abroad who trusted an Antiguan licence, the case showed that the island's supervision could be paid for. Thousands of savers lost their money in a bank that the regulator had been paid not to look at, and the case took a decade to reach a verdict.

Austria.d:
Austria sits between east and west, and Vienna has long been a base for foreign spy services. The documented reach-in now runs from Russia into Austria's own security state. The clearest illustration is a former officer of Austria's domestic intelligence agency, convicted in 2026 of working for Russia through Jan Marsalek, the fugitive former Wirecard executive: he used police databases to find people Moscow was looking for, including a journalist, and handed over work phones from the interior minister's office. He plans to appeal.

A second, quieter route is through international networks of future leaders. Sebastian Kurz, chancellor in 2017–19 and 2020–21, is listed as a member of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders network, which the Davos organisers run for people under 40. Being selected is not wrongdoing, and no inquiry has found that the network directed his government's decisions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Austria 4 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 7.5 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, especially exiles, journalists and others whom Russia's government wants to find, the main risk is that an official with access to state databases and ministers' phones may be working for a foreign service, which turns the state's own records into a way of locating them.

Bangladesh.d:
In Bangladesh two kinds of outsider have been documented reaching into the state: drug traffickers buying protection in the border district through which most methamphetamine pills enter the country, and an international Islamist movement reaching into the army.

Almost all yaba, a cheap methamphetamine pill made in Myanmar, enters Bangladesh through Cox's Bazar district, and the trade has paid local politicians and police there. The clearest sign is that the government's own list of yaba traffickers named the district's member of parliament. He was jailed in 2018 for hiding his wealth, but the trafficking claims never went to trial, and the following year 102 dealers, several of them his relatives, surrendered at a staged ceremony while the trade went on.

The second route is through the armed forces. In January 2012 the army announced it had stopped a coup attempt by serving and retired officers and named Hizb ut-Tahrir among those behind it; Hizb ut-Tahrir is an international movement that seeks a single Islamic state, or caliphate, and has been banned in Bangladesh since 2009.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Bangladesh 7 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 4 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people in Cox's Bazar, this means the elected representative and the police who are meant to control the drug trade have been tied to it, so a complaint about dealers may go to the people protecting them.

Belize.d:
No case of an outside party placing people or money inside Belize's government or companies remains on this map after checking. That is a statement about the documented record, not proof that none exists.

Belize sits between Mexico and Guatemala on the Caribbean coast, on routes used to move cocaine north from South America, and it offers offshore company registration. Those are the conditions under which outside money tends to look for officials willing to help. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Belize 5.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, in the middle of the range, but only about 3.6 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, which is weak.

For people living there, this means there is no documented case in which they can name an official acting for an outside party. The weak resilience score matters more: if traffickers or foreign buyers did reach officials, the courts, police and regulators that should catch it are rated as poorly placed to do so. The records that would show it first are the ownership of registered companies and how drug cases on the coast and the border are handled.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.d:
Bosnia and Herzegovina sits on the Balkan route by which cocaine and other drugs reach western Europe, and Balkan cocaine networks with bosses abroad use the country to move and clean their money. The documented pattern is those networks paying Bosnian officials to help.

The clearest illustration came in 2024, when police arrested 23 people in Sarajevo for trafficking and laundering money for the inner circle of a cocaine boss already sentenced in the Netherlands. Europol, the EU police agency, said those detained included corrupt officials who had worked for the group. The case is at the charging stage.

The country's divided government gives such networks room. Since the 1995 peace deal, power is split between two halves, the Federation and the Serb-run Republika Srpska, each with its own police and ministries, and between ethnic parties within them, so there are many separate offices a network can approach. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Bosnia 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests, among the highest in Europe, and about 3.9 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, among the lowest.

For people living there, this means an official handling their permit, case or complaint may also be working for a criminal network, and the bodies that should catch that are rated among the weakest on the continent. Residents dealing with the state cannot easily tell which officials answer to the public and which to a network whose leaders live abroad.

Bulgaria.d:
Bulgaria sits on the Balkan route, the main land route by which drugs and smuggled goods enter the European Union, and smugglers get through it by paying the customs officers and border police who are supposed to stop them. The protection reaches well above the checkpoint: when the United States sanctioned Bulgarian officials and business figures for shielding smuggling networks in 2021, it was the largest anti-corruption action of its kind Washington had taken against any single country, and several of those named held customs and border posts. Few of them have faced a Bulgarian prosecutor, and the same institutions still run the crossings.

The courts are the other place people try to reach. A man known as 'the Notary', Martin Bozhanov, is alleged to have gathered compromising files on judges and prosecutors and used them to pressure their decisions; the claims are under investigation and untested in court.

For people living here, this means goods crossing into the country without the checks the law requires, and, if the files allegations hold, cases decided by judges and prosecutors who answer to whoever holds material on them. The Global Organized Crime Index, which rates how far officials work for criminal interests, rates Bulgaria high, and its courts, police and watchdogs as only middling in their ability to push back. Because so few of the officials named abroad have been charged at home, residents have little evidence that a paid official ever loses the job.

Cambodia.d:
In Cambodia the people who run scam compounds have been brought inside the circle of power. The compounds are fenced sites where trafficked workers are held in debt bondage and forced to run online fraud against people abroad. Their owners have been given honorary titles, made advisers to the country's leaders and seated in its parliament, and successive US and British sanctions have named political protection as the reason the compounds operate in the open. Chen Zhi, founder of the Prince Group conglomerate, is the clearest example: he served as an official adviser to two prime ministers while, according to US prosecutors, his group ran such compounds, and in 2026 Cambodia stripped his citizenship and sent him to China. A sitting senator has also been sanctioned over the same trade.

Cambodian courts have prosecuted none of the people sanctioned abroad. That leaves the workers held in the compounds without any Cambodian court acting for them, and it means the people defrauded overseas, whose losses the US Treasury puts in the billions of dollars a year across Southeast Asia, are paying an industry whose owners sit beside the country's lawmakers.

Foreign religious movements have also courted the same leadership: the Unification Church's political arm gave Hun Sen awards while he was prime minister. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cambodia among the worst countries in the world for officials working for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs to push back.

Chad.d:
In Chad the documented reach runs through the drug trade and into the security services themselves. Tramadol, a prescription painkiller, is trafficked illegally across the Sahel, and the network moving it through Chad counted high-ranking army and intelligence officials among its members. Analysts who read the court papers when ten members were convicted in 2020 described large sums circulating among them, some used in attempts to bribe judges and the security services.

When army and intelligence officers are inside a trafficking network, the agencies meant to stop the trade include some of the people running it. Chadians then depend for protection on police and courts that the same network has tried to buy. The conviction shows the courts can act, but the Global Organized Crime Index rates Chad among the countries where officials most often work for criminal interests, and its courts, police and watchdogs among the weakest.

At the top of the state, Idriss Déby, president from 1990 to 2021, was named as a Freemason in press reports, alongside several other presidents of former French colonies in Central Africa. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges and swear oaths of mutual support. No lodge was named for Déby, and no decision of his is tied to it.

Comoros.d:
In Comoros, the documented outside reach into the state comes from a tobacco company. Leaked records from British American Tobacco (BAT) show the company arranging bribes for Comorian officials, part of a run of payments in several African countries that included efforts to block tobacco control laws based on the WHO tobacco treaty. A British fraud inquiry closed without charges and BAT denies wrongdoing.

For Comorians, if the tobacco payments worked as reported, they live under weaker limits on tobacco sales and advertising than the treaty sets. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Comoros high for officials working for criminal interests, with very weak courts, police and watchdogs.

Cote d'Ivoire.d:
What is documented for Côte d'Ivoire is Freemasonry among the officials who run the state's security and justice. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges under a national grand lodge. Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that the prime minister and the interior minister, who was responsible for the police, were Freemasons, and that the state prosecutor had been received by the Grande Loge de Côte d'Ivoire.

When the head of government, the minister over the police and the chief prosecutor share or attend the same private body, Ivorians cannot see whether that tie plays any part in who is appointed or who is prosecuted. The reporting does not show that it did, and lodge membership is lawful. The concern for residents is that if it did, there would be no public record of it.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Côte d'Ivoire high for officials working for criminal interests, with courts, police and watchdogs of middling strength. No documented case on the map shows a foreign state, company or criminal group paying Ivorian officials.

Czech Republic.d:
Outside reach into the Czech state has come from China and from the prime minister's own company. China has worked through business and the presidency: a former president took as his economic adviser the chairman of a Chinese energy company that was buying Czech assets, a man who had served in a Beijing body that builds contacts with foreigners on China's behalf.

The most direct case is at home.
