Prime Minister Andrej Babiš owns Agrofert, a farming, food and chemicals group that receives EU farm subsidies, and a European Commission audit found he still controlled it while in office and was in a conflict of interest. He returned as prime minister in 2025 and has moved the shares into a new trust, saying the conflict is resolved.

For Czechs, this means a head of government whose ministers set the rules and grants that reach his own company. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Czech officials low to middling for working with criminal interests, with relatively strong institutions.

Dominican Republic.d:
In the Dominican Republic outside money has reached officials through public works contracts and through the drug trade. Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction company, admitted paying $92 million in bribes in the country to win public works, and a former public works minister was convicted over it.

The drug trade reaches the agencies meant to stop it. The Dominican Republic is a transit point for cocaine bound for Puerto Rico and Europe, and traffickers have recruited officers of the National Drug Control Agency to guard their shipments and navy officers responsible for port security to move drugs through the ports. The purges show the scale: since 2009 the drug agency has removed hundreds of staff, many suspected of trafficking, and the national police has expelled well over a thousand officers.

For Dominicans, public works were paid for under contracts that carried tens of millions of dollars in bribes, and in ports and coastal areas some of the anti-drug agents and navy officers were working for the traffickers. The purges show the agencies are trying to remove them, and also how many there were. The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs.

Equatorial Guinea.d:
Equatorial Guinea is a small oil and gas producer on the Gulf of Guinea, ruled by Teodoro Obiang since 1979. Little is documented of outside groups getting inside its government, and what there is comes from the oil and commodity trade. Glencore, a Swiss-based commodity trader, pleaded guilty in Britain to paying bribes to officials in five African oil-producing countries, Equatorial Guinea among them, to win oil business.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 9 out of 10, among the highest anywhere, and the courts, police and watchdogs that would resist them at just over 2. That combination describes a state where the people in office control the main sources of money and there is no independent body to question how contracts are given out.

For people living there, oil revenue that could pay for services passes through officials whom foreign traders have shown they are willing to pay. With power held by one president for more than four decades and weak courts, Equatoguineans have no domestic route to find out who was paid or to hold anyone to account; the one documented case was brought by prosecutors abroad.

Ethiopia.d:
Very little is documented of outside forces getting inside Ethiopia's government. The one case on the map is about religion rather than money. Abiy Ahmed, prime minister since 2018, belongs to the Ethiopian Full Gospel Believers' Church, a Pentecostal church, and sometimes preaches there. He converted after the 1998–2000 war with Eritrea, and in 2019 he formed the Prosperity Party, which governs today. Pentecostal churches are a fast-growing Protestant movement in Ethiopia, which has long been mostly Orthodox Christian and Muslim. Religious belief is lawful, and no record shows the church directing government decisions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 6 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at 4.5, which suggests more is going on than has been documented. Ethiopia has been through civil war in Tigray and continuing conflict in Amhara and Oromia, which makes reporting on officials harder.

For Ethiopians, the documented picture is of a head of government whose faith ties him to a particular religious community in a country with several large faiths. Whether that shapes who is appointed or which policies are chosen has not been shown, and the weak watchdogs mean there is little official scrutiny of how decisions are made.

Gabon.d:
In Gabon, Freemasonry has been part of how the country is ruled. Freemasonry is a society of private lodges whose members swear oaths of mutual support; Gabon's two main lodges were founded by Omar Bongo, president from 1967 to 2009, and are tied to two French Masonic bodies, the Grand Orient de France and the Grande Loge Nationale Française. Omar Bongo led them until he died, and his son Ali Bongo was installed as grand master by the French lodge's own leader in the year he became president, keeping the post until after the 2023 coup. For most of the half-century from 1967 to 2023, the head of state was also the head of the country's lodges.

Lodge membership reached into the rest of the state too. Ministers and the head of the National Security Council attended Ali Bongo's installation, and a police chief led another of the country's lodges. After the 2023 coup the grand mastership went to a provincial governor when the coup leader, Brice Oligui Nguema, reportedly declined it, and the leader of the Grand Orient de France met him in secret in Libreville to offer support.

For people in Gabon this means that the president, ministers and security chiefs also met as lodge brothers, in meetings whose membership and decisions are private and connected to bodies in the former colonial power. Gabonese voters have no way to know what is agreed there or whether lodge ties decide who is appointed. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for outside or criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at 3.5.

Ghana.d:
In Ghana the documented network inside government is Freemasonry, a society of private lodges whose members pledge mutual support. Membership runs through the political class of both main parties: a former president has said he joined in 1967, ministers of the previous and current governments have taken part as members or confirmed membership when questioned in parliament, and the Asantehene, the king of the Asante and the country's most powerful traditional ruler, was honoured in 2024 for 25 years in the order. Membership is lawful.

The second pattern is cocaine moving through West Africa on its way to Europe, and the officers paid to let it pass. In 2006 a large cocaine load landed from a ship and then disappeared, and a senior police officer recorded meeting suspects at his home returned to duty after a judge-led inquiry found the police account unsatisfactory.

For Ghanaians this means ministers, the security chief and the country's leading traditional ruler share private loyalties that residents cannot see into, so people cannot tell whether lodge ties affect who is appointed. Traffickers have reached the police, and the officer involved in the lost cocaine kept his job, which leaves people unsure whether police will act against traffickers. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 5.3.

Guinea.d:
Guinea holds one of the world's largest untapped iron ore deposits, at Simandou, and the documented case of outside interests getting inside its government is about mining rights. In 2008 the government took two blocks of it from the mining company Rio Tinto and gave them to a company controlled by Israeli businessman Beny Steinmetz. A Swiss court later found that he got them by bribing a wife of President Lansana Conté; he denies wrongdoing. The deal shows how a foreign investor could win national resources by paying someone in the president's household rather than through open bidding.

The country's lodges are another channel to the top. In 2012 the magazine Jeune Afrique reported that President Alpha Condé oversaw the Grand Lodge of Guinea, the national body of Freemasonry, a society of private lodges whose membership is not made public.

For Guineans, the Simandou case meant that control of one of the world's largest untapped iron deposits was decided by a bribe, and years of potential state revenue were lost while the rights were contested. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 8 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at under 3, so cases like this tend to be pursued abroad, if at all.

Honduras.d:
Honduras is one of the main stopping points for cocaine flown and shipped from South America towards Mexico and the United States, and over the past two decades trafficking groups bought protection at the very top of the state. According to US courts, traffickers paid a president, his brother in Congress and a national police chief to let cocaine through, and trial evidence said drug money paid for the governing National Party's election campaigns. The clearest single case is Juan Orlando Hernández, president from 2014 to 2022, who was convicted in New York of protecting cocaine shipments and later released on a US pardon in 2025.

Trafficking groups also got inside the country's banks and business elite. A Honduran trafficking organisation, the Cachiros, laundered money through a bank owned by one of the country's most powerful political families, which regulators closed after the US sanctioned it.

For Hondurans, this means the police, Congress and presidency have all been used to move cocaine, and elections were partly paid for with drug money, according to US trial evidence. The main cases were tried abroad, and the former president was released, so Hondurans have not seen these officials tried at home. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at under 4.

Indonesia.d:
In Indonesia, outside forces have reached the state mainly through money and training. For most of Suharto's rule, which began in 1966, the planning agency and the finance ministry were run by a group of economists the Ford Foundation, a US charity, had paid to train at the University of California, Berkeley. This 'Berkeley Mafia' held those posts until 1983, cut inflation and opened the country to foreign investors, setting the terms on which outside capital came in.

Foreign companies selling to the state or seeking its approval have paid officials directly. Aircraft and engine makers paid the head of the state airline while he was buying from them, and a US seed company paid an environment ministry official who was assessing its genetically modified cotton; US regulators found that company's local affiliates had paid at least 140 officials or their relatives. In most such cases the facts came out through foreign prosecutors rather than Indonesian ones. Religion reaches the top by an open route: the leader of Nahdlatul Ulama, Indonesia's largest Muslim organisation, served as vice-president from 2019 to 2024.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Indonesia 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and below 5 for its courts and watchdogs. For Indonesians this means decisions on what their state buys and which crops reach their farms have been shaped by foreign firms' payments, and they have depended on other countries' courts to find out.

Israel.d:
In Israel the documented cases show private and foreign money reaching the prime minister's own circle. The route is through regulation and media: a business that needs decisions from the state can offer the politician who makes them something he wants in return, such as favourable news coverage. Prosecutors say that is what happened when Benjamin Netanyahu, as communications minister, gave valuable decisions to the owner of Israel's largest telecoms company, whose news site then covered him favourably; he denies it and has been on trial since 2020. Foreign states have also tried to buy a voice inside his office, and police are investigating two of his aides over money, routed through a US lobbying firm, to promote the image of Qatar, a Gulf state that hosts Hamas's political office. Netanyahu was questioned only as a witness and calls it a political witch hunt.

Organised crime reaches into the police from below. Israeli courts have convicted serving officers of passing investigation files to crime families, so that the families knew what cases were being built against them.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Israel 5.5 out of 10 both for officials working for criminal or outside interests and for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For people in Israel this means the news on a major website may have been shaped by a deal with the minister regulating its owner, and anyone who reports a crime family to the police cannot be sure their statement will stay inside the station.

Jordan.d:
In Jordan, outside pressure on the state comes from two directions: drug smugglers on the Syrian border and an Islamist movement that has worked through parliament. Smugglers moving captagon, an amphetamine pill made in Syria, need the border to stay open to them, so they recruit the people guarding it: serving and former soldiers have been convicted of carrying pills and weapons across.

The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement that works to bring its members into power, competed openly through its own party, the Islamic Action Front, which became the largest party in parliament in the 2024 election. In 2025 the government banned all of the Brotherhood's activities and said it would seize its assets, after arrests over an alleged weapons plot that the group said it knew nothing about.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Jordan 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and above 5 for its courts and watchdogs. For families in northern Jordan this means living on a smuggling route where some of the soldiers paid to stop the drugs have been caught moving them. For the voters who made the Islamic Action Front the largest party, it means their party's parent movement is now banned and its members face arrest.

Korea, DPR.d:
In North Korea the state itself is the organisation that crosses borders, and nothing on record shows an outside force inside its government. No case on this map documents a foreign state, crime group or company paying or placing North Korean officials.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives North Korea the worst possible score, 10 out of 10, for officials taking part in criminal activity, and one of the lowest anywhere for its courts and watchdogs. The US Justice Department has charged networks that placed thousands of North Korean IT workers, using stolen or fake identities, in remote jobs at foreign companies, with their wages paid into accounts controlled by the state to help fund its weapons programmes.

For people in North Korea this means the criminal schemes are run by their own government, and the money from overseas work goes to the state rather than to them. With no independent courts, press or watchdogs, they have no means of learning what is done in their name abroad or of challenging it at home.

Kyrgyzstan.d:
In Kyrgyzstan smuggling networks have reached into the state through the customs service, the office that decides what crosses the border and what duty is paid on it. A smuggling operation with people inside customs controls both what comes in unchecked and how much revenue the state loses. The clearest case is Raiymbek Matraimov, a deputy head of customs whom journalists tied to a scheme that moved hundreds of millions of dollars out of the country, and whom the US sanctioned in 2020; at home he settled by repaying money and served no prison term at the time.

The pattern extends to how the state treats those who expose it. Journalists from the organised-crime reporting network OCCRP and the Kyrgyz outlet Kloop, who documented the customs scheme, were prosecuted or forced out, while the official they wrote about stayed free.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kyrgyzstan 8.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For people in Kyrgyzstan this means customs revenue that should have paid for schools, roads and hospitals has left the country, the officials at the centre of it face little at home, and the reporters who tell them about it pay a higher price than the officials do.

Lesotho.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Lesotho, so this account is an estimate. No case found shows a foreign state, company, criminal group or lodge paying or placing people inside its government. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, has a documented presence, but nothing ties it to any decision.

The conditions suggest more than the record shows. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Lesotho 7 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, which means experts judge that officials are likely to act for criminal or outside interests and that there is little to stop them. The lack of cases may reflect thin reporting rather than an absence of influence.

For people in Lesotho this means pressure on officials, if it exists, would most likely show in contracts, licences and policing that ordinary residents cannot easily question, and they would pay for it through lost public money and weaker protection. Without a documented case there is no named official or company to hold to account.

Lithuania.d:
Lithuania's documented exposure has come through money from Russian business circles reaching its politicians, and through its own institutions catching it. The clearest case is the president removed in 2004: a Russian helicopter businessman who had funded his campaign was then granted Lithuanian citizenship by presidential decree, and the constitutional court and parliament together impeached him, the first European head of state removed that way.

That case set the pattern people in Lithuania have lived with since. The risk lies in decisions that rest with a single office, such as who receives citizenship, where one payment to one person can be enough. At the same time Lithuania's courts, prosecutors and parliament have shown they can act on it without outside help, and the Global Organized Crime Index rates those institutions as fairly strong while finding only a moderate level of officials serving criminal interests.

For Lithuanians this means the risk is less a captured state than a standing pressure on individual office-holders, which so far has come to light through their own courts rather than through foreign investigators.

Malaysia.d:
In Malaysia, outside money has reached the state at both ends: through international finance at the top of government, and through drug traffickers at the level of local police.

At the top, the problem ran through a state investment fund. 1MDB, set up to finance development, raised billions through bond sales arranged by Goldman Sachs bankers with the financier Jho Low, and US authorities say the money was diverted to bribe officials in Malaysia and the United Arab Emirates. The clearest result is the conviction of Najib Razak, prime minister until 2018, over more than 1 billion dollars found in his personal accounts; he is appealing. A state fund of this kind gives the people running it control of public money with little outside scrutiny, and foreign banks earned fees for raising it.

At street level, traffickers moving methamphetamine from the Golden Triangle, where Myanmar, Laos and Thailand meet, pay Malaysian narcotics officers to release suspects and to put seized drugs back on sale. The anti-corruption commission has prosecuted such officers repeatedly in recent years, most of them in Johor, near Singapore, and the Klang Valley around Kuala Lumpur. Malaysia hosts the region's busiest transhipment port, which makes its officers worth paying.

For Malaysians this means a public fund meant to pay for development was used to fill a prime minister's accounts, and the country carries the loss. People in Johor and the Klang Valley live where some of the officers paid to stop drugs have sold them back onto the street.

Marshall Islands.d:
The documented outside reach into the Marshall Islands is an attempt by foreign businesspeople to buy a law that would have given them their own territory. Two China-born businesspeople paid members of parliament and other officials over several years to pass a law creating a semi-autonomous 'special administrative region' on Rongelap Atoll. Both pleaded guilty in the United States, and the US government later barred a former Marshallese president and an MP from entering the country for taking the bribes; the former president denies it.

The scheme shows how a small Pacific state can be approached. A parliament of a few dozen members meant that paying a handful of lawmakers could move a law. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a relatively low level of officials serving outside interests in the Marshall Islands, which fits a country where this was a single scheme rather than a settled arrangement.

For the people of Rongelap this means lawmakers were paid to put their home under a separate set of rules written for the buyers. No one has been charged in the Marshall Islands, so the case was settled in a foreign court, and Marshallese have no ruling of their own on which officials took money.

Micronesia.d:
What is documented for the Federated States of Micronesia is an accusation made by its own head of state. In 2023, shortly before leaving office, President David Panuelo wrote a long letter saying China was using bribery and threats against Micronesian officials as 'political warfare', with the aim of keeping the Pacific country on Beijing's side, or neutral, if war broke out over Taiwan. He wrote that he had considered switching diplomatic recognition from China to Taiwan. China rejected the claims, no court or inquiry has tested them, and no official has been named as taking money.

The method described is one suited to a small state: a government of a few dozen senior officials decides which of China or Taiwan it recognises and how it votes abroad, so paying or pressing a handful of them can move the whole country's foreign policy. What China would gain, if the account is true, is a Pacific government that stays friendly or neutral in a war over Taiwan. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a relatively low level of officials serving outside interests in Micronesia.

For Micronesians, if the president's account is true, some of their officials have made decisions on foreign policy and security after taking money or giving way to threats from abroad. Because nothing has been investigated, they cannot tell which officials, if any, were involved, or whether later choices about Taiwan and defence were made freely.

Montenegro.d:
In Montenegro, organised crime has had protectors at the top of the justice system itself. Montenegrin clans that trade cocaine, such as the Kavac clan, have needed judges, prosecutors and police chiefs who will look away or tip them off, and messages from Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service used by criminals that police cracked, have exposed how far this reached. Since those messages were passed to Montenegro by Europol, the EU's police agency, former heads of the Supreme Court, the special prosecution office and the police, along with security officers and a coastal mayor, have been charged with protecting crime groups. The clearest case is the former Supreme Court president convicted in 2026 of using her position to shield a smuggling network run by her son.

Separately, the prime minister was named in 2025 to the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses for people under about 40 run by the organisation behind the Davos meetings, which works to shape government policy through cooperation between companies and states.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Montenegro widely serving criminal interests. For people there this means that the judges, prosecutors and police chiefs they would turn to were, in several cases, working for the groups they were meant to pursue, and anyone whose case reached the Supreme Court in those years cannot be sure it was heard fairly. Most of these charges are still unproven, and the evidence came from messages decrypted by foreign police rather than from Montenegro's own institutions.

Namibia.d:
In Namibia, the documented outside reach is through the country's natural resources, where a foreign company is alleged to have bought access from the ministers who control it. Namibia's fish belong to the public, and the government hands out quotas, licences to catch a set amount. In the case known as 'Fishrot', leaked files published in 2019 showed that Samherji, one of Iceland's largest fishing companies, had paid people close to the government to obtain horse-mackerel quotas. The fisheries and justice ministers resigned and were arrested with several associates, and they face racketeering, corruption and money-laundering charges under Namibia's organised crime law. Samherji denies paying bribes, and no one has yet been convicted.

The mechanism is one seen wherever a few ministers control who may take a public resource such as fish, timber or minerals: a foreign company that pays those ministers or their associates can be given a share that would otherwise go to local firms or be sold for the public's benefit. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a moderate-to-high level of officials serving outside interests in Namibia and rates its institutions as fairly weak.

For Namibians, if the charges are proved, two ministers sold a public resource to a foreign company. Local fishing firms and their workers lost quota they would otherwise have had, and the state lost income that would have gone to the public budget. The trial has run for years, so people still wait for a court to say who took part.

New Zealand.d:
In New Zealand the documented reach into government comes from two directions. The Chinese state has had people in Parliament whose ties to it were known to the intelligence services but not to voters, and international free-market and business networks have counted finance ministers, prime ministers and deputy prime ministers among their members.

The parliamentary side shows in how such cases end. When the intelligence agencies raised concerns about MPs' relationships with the Chinese government, the matter was settled quietly between party leaders and the MPs retired at an election; the clearest example is Jian Yang, a National MP who had been a Communist Party member and had taught at Chinese army schools that trained intelligence linguists. Voters had elected and re-elected him without being told, and learned the reason for his departure only from the press afterwards.

The network side works through training and contacts rather than money. The Mont Pelerin Society, a club founded to spread free-market ideas into policy, the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme, and the Atlas Network, a US-based body that funds and trains free-market think tanks, have each had a member in one of New Zealand's top economic or political offices over the past three decades. Membership is lawful and no inquiry has found that any of these groups directed a New Zealand decision, but residents have no public record of what is discussed inside them.

Organised crime has little hold on officials here: the Global Organized Crime Index gives New Zealand one of the world's lowest scores for officials working for criminal interests.

North Macedonia.d:
North Macedonia has little documented outside infiltration of its government, and what there is comes through a private international forum rather than through money or crime. The World Economic Forum, the Swiss-based organisation behind the annual Davos meeting, works to shape policy through cooperation between companies and governments, and its Young Global Leaders programme draws rising officials into a five-year network of meetings with business leaders. The country's current minister of foreign affairs and foreign trade, Timčo Mucunski, joined it in 2025.

Taking part is lawful and no inquiry has found that the Forum directed his decisions. For people in North Macedonia it means that the minister who negotiates their trade deals belongs to a network where company executives can meet him at events whose discussions are not published, so residents have no record of what is raised there or whether it reaches policy.

The Global Organized Crime Index places North Macedonia in its moderate band, with a fairly high score for officials working for criminal or outside interests and middling strength in its courts, police and watchdogs. That suggests more room for outside influence than the documented record shows, and this account covers only what has come to light.

Palau.d:
Palau's documented case shows how a criminal group can reach a small state's government through the front door of business and goodwill. In Pacific island states, organised crime groups from Macau and Hong Kong arrive as investors and cultural associations, ask local officials to sit on their boards, and propose casinos or special economic zones that would sit partly outside national law.

The clearest example is Wan Kuok-koi, known as 'Broken Tooth', a former head of Macau's 14K triad whom the US Treasury sanctioned in 2020. Immigration records reported by OCCRP, a network of investigative journalists, show he was listed as a 'guest of the government' on a visit in 2018–19, and a serving postmaster general and a state governor became directors of his Palau association, which planned a casino zone on Angaur island where he would control customs, ports and an airport. It stopped in 2019 when the president, warned by Taiwan of Wan's record, came out against it, and the association applied to dissolve. OCCRP did not establish that the Chinese state directed the effort, and no one in Palau has been charged.

For a country of about 18,000 people, two serving officials lending their names gave a sanctioned gang leader local standing, and one island came close to hosting a casino zone under his control. What stopped it was a presidential decision on a foreign government's warning, not a law that blocked it.

Peru.d:
In Peru, foreign builders have bought presidents, judges have sold rulings from inside the system, and religious and fraternal networks keep a steady place in cabinet and city hall.

The foreign money came mainly from Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group that admitted paying bribes in a dozen countries to win public contracts. In Peru that money reached presidents and their campaigns, and two former presidents have been sentenced over it, one for taking about $35 million in return for the contract to build the Interoceanic Highway. Peruvians paid for public works whose contracts were awarded in return for bribes, and for years the people at the head of the state owed something to a foreign contractor.

Inside the courts, the reach has come through networks of judges, prosecutors and the officials who appoint them, trading sentence reductions and promotions among themselves and with outsiders. Wiretaps released in 2018 recorded a supreme court judge and members of the council that appointed judges doing exactly that. People who went before a Peruvian court in those years could not be sure the outcome had not been arranged.

Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members carry their faith into public life, has had members serving as ministers and as mayor of Lima, and Freemasons, members of a fraternity of private lodges, have been reported among senior officials; membership is lawful and no finding links either to a specific decision. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Peru high for officials working for criminal interests.

Qatar.d:
Qatar's documented case runs outward, with Qatar's own money reported to have reached inside another country's government. Israeli prosecutors are investigating aides of the Israeli prime minister over money reported to have come from Qatar to promote its image from inside his office.

Qatar's residents have no elected body able to ask how state money is spent abroad. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Qatar fairly high for officials working for criminal or outside interests.

Samoa.d:
No case of outside groups paying or placing officials in Samoa is documented yet, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions. The only outside organisation recorded as present is Shincheonji Church of Jesus, a South Korean religious movement, and its presence is lawful and not evidence of wrongdoing.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Samoa in its low band, scoring it low for officials working for criminal or outside interests and in the middle range for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. Neighbouring Pacific states have seen bribes for business deals, and small island governments with few investigators are the kind of place where such pressures can go unnoticed.

For residents, the absence of cases means there is no specific harm to point to, not that none exists. The bodies that would bring such cases to light, the courts, police and audit office, are the ones whose middling scores leave that question open.

Senegal.d:
In Senegal the strongest outside force inside politics is a religious one that comes from within the country: the Sufi brotherhoods, above all the Mourides, whose leader, the Khalife général, commands the loyalty of millions of followers. Their holy city, Touba, has run its own affairs with wide autonomy since 1928, and presidents court the Khalife: a visit before the yearly Grand Magal pilgrimage has become customary, and newly elected presidents have gone to Touba within days, some putting Mourides in their governments. For Senegalese, this means decisions about spending in Touba, such as its water and sanitation, are agreed between the president and a religious leader no one elected.

Foreign religious movements have reached the presidency too. The Unification Church, a Korean-founded church, gave its $1 million Sunhak Peace Prize to President Macky Sall in 2020 while he was in office, and press reports have named past presidents as Freemasons, members of a fraternity whose members meet in private lodges, which one of them denied.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Senegal in the middle range both for officials working for criminal interests and for the strength of its courts and watchdogs.

Singapore.d:
Singapore's government treats foreign influence, most often linked to China, as something that works through ordinary community life: business chambers, clan and grassroots associations and universities. Its response is to name the people it believes are being used, and it does this by ministerial decision, not by trial. In 2017 it expelled a US-citizen professor at the state university's public-policy school as an 'agent of influence' working with an unnamed foreign intelligence service, which he denied. Since 2024 a foreign-interference law lets it designate residents, so far a business-chamber leader who had attended a Chinese Communist Party united front body, and make them report each year their political donations and foreign ties.

The city is also a base from which other governments are reached. For years a Singapore ship-supply firm run by Leonard Francis bribed US Navy officers with cash, travel and gifts for ship schedules and inside information, while a civilian Navy contracting officer in Singapore stopped an early inquiry; US prosecutors charged 33 people.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 1.5 out of 10, among the lowest in the world, and courts and watchdogs at about 7.8. For residents the trade-off is plain: people who lead community or business groups with ties to China can be publicly named and made to disclose their links, and a resident can lose the right to live here on a ministry's word without hearing the evidence in court.

Somalia.d:
In Somalia the outside force reaching furthest into the state is al-Shabaab, the armed Islamist group fighting the federal government, which places its own people inside the government it is trying to overthrow. Its members take public jobs, sometimes under false names, to collect information for taxing businesses and choosing targets; defectors are often taken into the security forces without vetting, and analysts warn that the intelligence service includes former members. In 2019 the governor of the Benadir region, which includes Mogadishu, was killed by a suicide bomber who had got a job in his own office. The government has also dissolved a Chamber of Commerce board after finding the group's representatives on it.

Alongside the state's tax system the group runs its own. A UN panel of experts described 'mafia-style' taxation at Mogadishu's port and markets, and the Mogadishu-based Hiraal Institute estimated in 2020 that it raised close to as much as the government, from traders, farmers, travellers at checkpoints and containers at the port.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 1.9, among the weakest anywhere. For people in Somalia that means paying tax twice, to the government and to the group fighting it, and working in offices where a colleague may be passing on who should be taxed or killed.

Sri Lanka.d:
In Sri Lanka the reach into the state comes less from foreign governments than from a religious nationalist movement that presidents have brought into government. Bodu Bala Sena ('Buddhist Power Force') is a group of Sinhala Buddhist nationalist monks, founded in 2012 and accused of stirring violence against Muslims. Senior members of the Rajapaksa family, who dominated Sri Lankan politics for most of the past two decades, appeared at its events, and in 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa put its leader, the monk Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara, in charge of a presidential task force to draft proposals for a single legal code. The justice minister said he had not been consulted, and the Bar Association said the task force was taking over the work of Parliament and the Justice Ministry.

Foreign ideological networks are present too, at a more distant level. Ranil Wickremesinghe, prime minister several times and president from 2022 to 2024, is named as a member of the Mont Pelerin Society, an international society of free-market economists, but no one has found that it directed his decisions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 3.7. For Sri Lanka's Muslims, that pattern meant watching a monk accused of preaching against them handed the job of proposing how the country's laws should treat everyone, through a body that bypassed the elected parliament.

Sudan.d:
In Sudan an Islamist movement placed its members through the army, the civil service and the courts for thirty years, and it is still inside the state during the current war. The National Islamic Front, Hassan al-Turabi's movement derived from the Muslim Brotherhood, took power in 1989 through supporters in the army, who brought Omar al-Bashir to power in a coup. Under his rule the movement filled state jobs with its own people, including judges and prosecutors.

When Bashir fell in 2019, a committee set up by the transitional government began removing the people placed under him and dismissed judges and court staff, but the courts ordered some of them back to work. The movement's leaders, including Bashir's former foreign minister, now head the Islamic Movement and are under US, Canadian and EU sanctions for blocking the move to civilian rule. Since the war between the army and the Rapid Support Forces began in 2023, the US Treasury says Islamists tied to Iran hold posts in the army-backed government, including the finance minister, and that a militia of up to 20,000 fighters beside the army was trained and armed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards; these are sanctions, not court findings.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8.5 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at about 2.3. For people in Sudan this means the courts and ministries they deal with are still staffed by people placed by one political movement, and the war fought through their towns is partly armed from abroad through the factions inside the government.

Syria.d:
Until December 2024 the drug trade in Syria was not something that had bought its way into the state; it was run by the state. Captagon, an amphetamine pill smuggled across the Middle East and the Gulf, was made and moved by people at the centre of the Assad government, and Syria produced about 80% of the world's supply, according to the British government. The UK, the US and the EU sanctioned the president's brother Maher al-Assad, whose army unit they said facilitated production and distribution, along with cousins of the president, militia leaders and businesspeople.

The trade also sat inside the legislature: Amer Khiti, a sitting member of parliament, was sanctioned in 2023 over companies that produced, packaged and moved the pills. These are sanctions imposed by foreign governments, not court verdicts, and the drug charges have never been tried; the former president and his brother live in Russia.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives Syria the highest possible score, 10 out of 10, for state-embedded crime, and about 2 for the strength of courts, police and watchdogs. For people in Syria this meant that the police and courts answered to the same people who ran the drug factories, so the trade could not be stopped from inside. Independent estimates cited by the British government put the captagon trade at up to $57 billion, and that money went to the ruling family and its army units rather than to the public.

Thailand.d:
In Thailand criminal businesses reach into the state through the police and the legislature, and the protection they buy is the same whether the money comes from drugs or from gambling. Thailand borders Myanmar's Shan State, one of the largest methamphetamine and heroin producing areas in the world, and networks linked to it move money into Thai property and politics.

In 2023 a sitting senator was indicted on drug trafficking and money-laundering charges tied to a Myanmar businessman whom the United States had sanctioned for supporting Myanmar's military government, and Thailand's narcotics board seized property worth over 400 million baht from homes connected to his family; the case has not reached a verdict. The same year Thailand's deputy national police chief was removed and investigated over alleged protection of an online gambling network, a case that split the police leadership in public.

International elite networks are also present, at a different level: the prime minister removed by the Constitutional Court in 2025, Paetongtarn Shinawatra, had been named to the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme while in office. Selection is not a finding of wrongdoing.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 5. For people in Thailand this means a senator charged over drug money helped vote on their laws, and when a deputy police chief is accused of protecting gambling operators, residents cannot be sure which complaints to the police will be followed up.

Trinidad and Tobago.d:
Little is documented of outside groups placing people inside Trinidad and Tobago's government, so this account is partly an estimate. The one recorded case shows how a private international body can end up with its own senior figure inside a national cabinet.

Jack Warner was a vice-president of FIFA, world football's governing body, and head of its regional confederation for North and Central America and the Caribbean, while he served as works minister and then national security minister until 2013. US prosecutors later charged him with taking bribes in his football roles, including a $10 million payment tied to South Africa's World Cup bid; FIFA banned him for life, and in 2025 Trinidad's High Court blocked his extradition, so the charges have never been tried.

The Global Organized Crime Index places the country in its Moderate band, scoring both officials acting for criminal interests and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5 out of 10. For people in Trinidad and Tobago this means one minister responsible for the police and security services was at the same time an officer of an outside organisation later accused of selling votes. Because the case cannot be tried at home or abroad, residents have no court finding on what that dual role cost them, and no other documented case to judge how common such arrangements are.

Tuvalu.d:
No case of outside groups paying or placing officials in Tuvalu is documented, so this account is an estimate based on conditions. Tuvalu is a nation of about 11,000 people on low-lying atolls, and its government depends heavily on foreign aid and on agreements with larger partners. Elsewhere in the Pacific, payments for business deals have drawn smaller states into larger powers' rivalries; none of this is documented in Tuvalu.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Tuvalu in its Minimal band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 1.5 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at 5.9. For Tuvaluans this means there is no known current harm from hidden outside influence. The risk is that a country this small has only a handful of officials, auditors and police, so if an outside interest did reach in, there would be few people in a position to notice it.

United Kingdom.d:
In Britain most outside influence works through access rather than cash. Companies and their advisers get inside the departments that regulate them: the big accounting firms have lent their tax staff to the Treasury to help draft tax law that the same firms then advise clients on, and during the pandemic, suppliers recommended by ministers and peers were sent through a fast-track 'VIP lane' for protective-equipment contracts.

Private fraternities sit inside the justice system. Freemasons, members of a fraternity whose members pledge to help one another, have long held posts in the police and courts; MPs estimated in 1999 that 5 to 10% of judges were masons. London's Metropolitan Police now requires officers to declare membership, and the High Court upheld that rule in 2026.

Foreign states work through politicians and their staff. MI5 warned MPs in 2022 that a solicitor who funded an MP's office was working covertly for China's United Front Work Department, the Communist Party body that builds influence abroad, and a former Welsh member of the European Parliament was jailed in 2025 for taking money to make pro-Russian speeches. Organised crime groups have paid serving police and prison officers for information and to move contraband, exposed only when police read the criminals' own encrypted messages.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Britain at 3 out of 10 and its courts, police and watchdogs at 7.6, among the strongest. For people in Britain, the risk lies mainly in rules written with the help of those they apply to: taxpayers paid for pandemic equipment that went unused, and a person reporting a crime cannot always know whether the officer handling it belongs to a lodge, or is on a crime group's payroll.

Vanuatu.d:
No case of outside groups placing people inside Vanuatu's government or paying its officials is documented, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Vanuatu at 3 out of 10, a low score, but scores its courts, police and watchdogs at only 4.9, in the middle of the range. That means experts judge that officials are not often working for criminal or outside interests, but that the bodies meant to catch it if they were are only moderately able to do so.

For ni-Vanuatu, as the country's people are called, the absence of cases means there is no named official or company to hold to account, not proof that none exists. With courts and watchdogs in the middle of the range, it would take time for any hidden outside influence on officials to come to light.

Yemen.d:
Yemen has been at war since 2014, and its government is now in large part a coalition of armed factions, each backed by a foreign power. The clearest case of outside placement is the Southern Transitional Council (STC), a movement seeking a separate southern state that was formed in 2017 with help from the United Arab Emirates. In 2022 the STC joined Yemen's eight-member Presidential Leadership Council, the country's top governing body, and its leader became a vice-president, so the UAE's client sat at the head of the state.

That arrangement broke down at the end of 2025, when the STC launched an offensive in the south and Saudi-backed forces struck back; its leader fled to the UAE in January 2026 and was removed from the council.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Yemen's courts, police and watchdogs at 1.9 out of 10, one of the lowest scores in the world, and officials acting for criminal interests at 8. For Yemenis, this means that decisions about who governs their region, who collects their taxes and who controls the ports are made by armed groups whose funding and orders come from Abu Dhabi, Riyadh or Tehran. When those patrons fall out, as in late 2025, civilians are caught in the fighting, and there is no court or police force they can turn to when an armed group backed from outside takes their land or money.

Algeria.d:
In Algeria the documented reach-in runs from the cocaine trade into the security state. Shipments coming through the port of Oran have needed protection, and when 701 kilograms of cocaine were found there in 2018 hidden in a cargo of imported meat, press reports tied the importer to judges, prosecutors, mayors and the children of senior politicians.

The seizure brought down the head of the national police, and he and several generals were later convicted of corruption and illicit enrichment. Those convictions were about personal wealth, not drugs. Algeria has published little about the trafficking itself, so the public record shows senior officers growing rich at the time a trafficking network was operating through a state port, without explaining in court how the two connect.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Algeria 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 4 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For Algerians, this means the people at the top of the police have been punished for wealth they could not explain while the question of who protected the cocaine moving through Oran has not been answered in public, and residents have no court account of which officials were paid to let shipments through or whether they are still in post.

Argentina.d:
In Argentina several kinds of outsider have reached into the state, and each has left a mark that is still felt. In the 1970s it was P2, a secret Masonic lodge run by the Italian businessman Licio Gelli. Membership lists seized in Italy in 1981 named an interim president, the ministers of social welfare, foreign affairs and the economy, the head of the joint chiefs of staff, a member of the military junta and several ambassadors, and Perón's government gave Gelli an Argentine diplomatic post. Several of those named went on to run the army or the death squads of the dictatorship years.

Today the reach-in is mostly through money and ideas. Free-market think tanks linked to the Atlas Network, a US-based group that funds and trains such think tanks worldwide, merged into one president's party and, by the network's own account, helped shape the next president's deregulation, tax and labour reforms. The economy ministry and the central bank are run by former JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank executives. Prosecutors also say construction and energy firms paid cash to officials of the previous government in return for public works contracts, and that case is now at trial.

Drug traffickers reach lower down. Courts have convicted a former head of the Santa Fe provincial police and federal judges in the north of protecting traffickers or selling them rulings. For people around Rosario, where the murder rate has run several times the national figure, that means the police commander or judge who should stand between them and the gangs may be on the gangs' side, while nationally the rules on prices, wages and public spending are shaped by people tied to foreign banks and think tanks.

Azerbaijan.d:
Azerbaijan's economy rests on oil and gas, and the state oil company, SOCAR, is closely bound up with the government. The documented pattern runs outward: the oil sector reaches into the international bodies that set rules affecting it, and Azerbaijani money has reached into European institutions that judge the country's record.

The clearest case is the UN climate summit, COP29, which Azerbaijan hosted in 2024. The summit's president had been a SOCAR vice-president, and its chief executive, a deputy energy minister, was secretly filmed by campaigners posing as investors discussing possible oil and gas deals in the run-up to the talks; critics said this broke the rule that a host must act impartially. Earlier, an independent inquiry for the Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly, the body that monitors human rights across the continent, reported in 2018 a strong suspicion that some of its members had acted for Azerbaijan in return for money or gifts, a practice that became known as caviar diplomacy.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Azerbaijan 8.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 4 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, this means the officials who decide on oil and gas deals also represented the country in talks meant to cut fossil fuel use, and the European bodies that are supposed to report honestly on their rights have themselves been targets of their government's money.

Barbados.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Barbados, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case shows an outside government, company, crime group or lodge paying officials or placing people in office on the island, and no outside organisation is recorded as present. The United Grand Lodge of England, Britain's main Masonic body, is thought to have lodges there, which is lawful and not confirmed.

The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, gives Barbados 3 out of 10 on that measure, low by world standards. It gives about 6.1 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, which is better than most of the Caribbean. Barbados is also an offshore financial centre that registers international companies, which is the kind of business that can draw outside money.

For people living there, this means no named official or company can be shown to be acting for an outside party, and the index suggests officials face less of this pressure than in many states. If outside money did reach in, it would most likely show up in who funds politicians, who wins public contracts and who owns the companies registered on the island, and residents are best protected when those records are public.

Benin.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Benin, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, criminal group or lodge paying or placing people inside its government. Two French Masonic bodies, the Grand Orient de France and the Grande Loge Nationale Française, are thought to have members in Benin but are not documented.

Benin is a coastal West African state whose port at Cotonou handles goods for its larger neighbour, Nigeria, and for landlocked states to the north, so much of the trade that crosses it belongs to outsiders. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Benin 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3.8 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That combination describes officials under real pressure and weak checks on them.

For people living there, this means that if outside interests are paying or placing officials, it is likely to show up in port and customs work, public contracts and policing, and residents would pay through lost public revenue and weaker protection. With no named case, there is no official or company they can yet challenge.

Botswana.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Botswana, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, criminal group, church or lodge paying or placing people inside its government, and no outside organisation is recorded as present.

Botswana's economy rests on diamonds, mined mainly through a long-standing partnership between the government and the De Beers company, and on that kind of single, valuable export outside interests often seek influence. Against that, the Global Organized Crime Index scores Botswana 4.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 5.4 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That puts it in the middle of the range and ahead of most of its neighbours. The lack of cases may also reflect limited investigative reporting.

For people living there, this means there is no named official or company to hold to account, and no evidence that public decisions are being bought. If a case exists, it would most likely surface through mining and other licences, public contracts or policing of the borders, and those are the records residents would need to see.

Burkina Faso.d:
What is documented for Burkina Faso is Freemasonry at the top of the government that ran the country until 2014. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges under a national grand lodge, led by an elected grand master. Under Blaise Compaoré, who ruled from 1987 to 2014, the presidency and the foreign ministry were linked through the Grande Loge du Burkina: the magazine Jeune Afrique reported that Compaoré had been its grand master and that his foreign minister, Djibrill Bassolé, succeeded him in that post.

In those years, the two men who set the country's foreign policy led, one after the other, a private body whose meetings and membership are closed to the public. Lodge membership is lawful, and the reporting does not show any decision taken for the lodge. What it shows is a tie between the people running the state and a network Burkinabè voters had no way to see into or question.

The record does not reach into the present military government. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Burkina Faso high for officials working for criminal interests and very weak in the courts, police and watchdogs that would check them, so outside influence on officials would meet little resistance at home, but no current case of it is documented here.

Cameroon.d:
The documented case in Cameroon reaches into the presidency itself, which Paul Biya has held since 1982. Le Monde reported that in his early years Biya passed tens of millions of French francs, some of it from the state oil company, to esoteric orders styled on the medieval Knights Templar and to the personal account of their French leader, Raymond Bernard. The presidency called Bernard an 'old friend' and declined to comment.

If that reporting is right, oil revenue that belongs to the public went to the head of a private spiritual order abroad rather than into the state budget, and the decision was made at the very top. Cameroonians have never had an official account of those payments, and the same man still holds office, so there is no route by which an inquiry would start from inside the government.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cameroon among the countries where officials most often work for criminal interests, and its courts, police and watchdogs as weak. On those terms, money moved out of a state company by the presidency is unlikely to be traced or recovered by Cameroon's own institutions.

Chile.d:
In Chile, outside reach has come mostly through ideas and the people trained in them. A US-funded exchange, paid for by US aid and later the Ford Foundation, trained more than a hundred Chilean economists at the University of Chicago from the 1950s to the 1970s. Known as the 'Chicago Boys', they wrote the economic plan General Pinochet's military government adopted and then ran its economic ministries and the central bank, so the country's economy was rebuilt on their programme.

Money has reached politicians directly. SQM, a lithium and fertiliser miner whose main shareholder is Pinochet's former son-in-law, paid campaigns across the political spectrum through fake invoices, and it now shares the country's lithium with the state copper company. In Santiago and the north, as Chile has become a drug transit route, officers of the Carabineros, the national police, have been charged with reselling seized drugs and protecting dealers. For Chileans, that means politicians whose campaigns a mining company paid, and police who in some places work for the trade they are meant to stop. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Chile's officials and institutions in the middle of the global range.

Congo, Dem. Rep..d:
In eastern Congo a neighbouring state has taken over the machinery of government. M23, an armed group, took the cities of Goma and Bukavu in early 2025, and UN sanctions monitors reported that Rwanda's army commands it and that it has set about dismantling state authority: it appointed new provincial governors, put Rwandans in charge of mining, tax, banking and border control, and removed customary chiefs. Rwanda denies directing M23.

Across the rest of the country, the reach has come through mining. Foreign investors and commodity traders have won mining and oil rights by paying officials or by personal ties to the presidency. The US Treasury sanctioned Dan Gertler, an Israeli investor and friend of former president Joseph Kabila, saying he made a fortune from corrupt mining and oil deals obtained through that friendship, and Glencore, one of Congo's largest miners, agreed to pay the state $180 million to settle claims that it bribed Congolese officials. Both deny wrongdoing.

For people in the Kivus, the governors, tax collectors and border officers over them are now appointed by an armed group backed by another country, and the chiefs they relied on are gone. Across Congo, mining wealth that should have reached the state budget went to insiders, and some came back only after foreign investigations forced settlements. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Congo among the very worst in the world for officials working for criminal interests, with little capacity at home to resist.

Croatia.d:
Croatia's documented case is a foreign company buying control of a national asset through the head of government. MOL, a Hungarian oil company in which the Hungarian state has influence, wanted to run INA, Croatia's national oil company, and Croatian courts found that Prime Minister Ivo Sanader took a 10 million euro bribe from MOL's chief executive to give it that control. MOL denies the bribe, and Hungary has not handed the executive over to Croatia.

For Croatians, the national oil company they part-own is still managed by the firm the courts found paid their prime minister for that control, and his conviction did not change who runs it. Croatian courts could punish the official who took the money but not the executive who paid it, because he lives in another EU country that will not send him back. The case shows a gap in how Europe deals with this kind of reach: the country that is harmed can try its own politicians, but the company and its managers stay out of reach.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Croatia in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. The conviction shows those courts can reach a former head of government, though it took them most of a decade.

Denmark.d:
Very little outside reach into the Danish state is documented on the map. The one remaining case is a network membership at the head of state: King Frederik X is listed among alumni of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme, which he joined as crown prince. The World Economic Forum is the Swiss-based organisation behind the annual Davos meeting of business and political leaders, and it works to shape government policy through cooperation between companies and states; its Young Global Leaders programme gathers people under about 40 into a five-year network of meetings and courses.

Denmark's king has a ceremonial role and does not set policy, so the membership does not show the Forum deciding anything for Danes. What it shows is that the Forum's network reaches into the institution that formally heads the Danish state.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Denmark among the very lowest countries in the world for officials working for criminal interests, and among the strongest for its courts, police and watchdogs. For residents, that means the officials they deal with are unlikely to be working for criminal or foreign interests, and the record here reflects that.

Ecuador.d:
Ecuador sits between the two largest cocaine-producing countries, Colombia and Peru, and its Pacific ports have become one of the main exits for cocaine bound for Europe and the United States. The trafficking groups that run this trade pay the officials who could stop it. At the coast they recruit port workers and customs officers so that drugs hidden in banana shipments leaving Guayaquil pass inspection. Inland they buy judges, prosecutors, police commanders and prison officials, so that members are released, cases are delayed and sentences are cut by judges who have no power to cut them. When one trafficker's phone was decrypted, the messages on it led to the conviction of 20 people, among them the former head of the council that oversees Ecuador's judges.

Foreign companies reach in by a different route, through the money. Foreign oil traders and builders have paid officials at Petroecuador, the state oil company, and in the ministries that oversee it, for contracts and confidential information, and those bribes have reached as high as a sitting vice-president, now in prison. Guillermo Lasso, president until 2023, has been reported as a married lay member of Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation; no case shows it steering his government.

For people in Ecuador this means a court ruling may have been bought, a gang leader may walk out of prison on a paid order, and the port and police staff around them may be on a gang's payroll. The bribes at Petroecuador came out of oil sales that pay for the state's schools and hospitals. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials working for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10, with the courts and watchdogs meant to resist them at under 4.5.

Eritrea.d:
This is an estimate: no case on the map names a foreign government, company or criminal group placing or paying people inside Eritrea's government. Eritrea has been governed by one party, the People's Front for Democracy and Justice, since independence in 1993, has held no national election in that time and has no independent press, so very little can be checked from outside.

What reporting there is points to criminal business run from inside the state rather than reaching in from outside. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 9.5 out of 10, one of the highest scores in the world, and says military officers and ruling-party members dominate smuggling of people, gold, alcohol, tobacco and counterfeit goods, much of it across the border with Sudan, and that officials involved are rarely prosecuted. A 2013 report presented at the European Parliament said the army's border surveillance unit took part in smuggling Eritreans into Sudan, where thousands are reported to have died in captivity.

If that picture is right, Eritreans who try to leave the country pay the same officers who are meant to guard the border, and money from gold and trade ends up in private hands. The strength of courts and watchdogs scores 2.2 out of 10, and there is no independent body inside the country where a resident could take a complaint.

Fiji.d:
Fiji sits on the shipping and air routes that carry methamphetamine and cocaine across the Pacific to Australia and New Zealand, and traffickers moving those drugs have got inside its police and customs. The minister for policing told parliament in November 2025 that 27 police officers had been involved in drug cases since the start of 2023. In one of them, two officers of the police counter-narcotics unit and a senior customs manager were charged with helping methamphetamine through Nadi airport in air cargo, and the unit was later disbanded. Leaked chats published in late 2025 appeared to show senior officers, including the head of the organised crime department, discussing drug shipments and payments with traffickers; the police commissioner confirmed an investigation, and the claims have not been tested in court.

For people in Fiji, this means the officers responsible for stopping drugs at the airport and the border may be working for those bringing them in. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 4 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 5.4, a middle position in which cases are being investigated and charged rather than ignored.

Gambia.d:
Under Yahya Jammeh, president from 1994 to 2017, The Gambia's state businesses were handed to a small circle around him, and part of that circle was tied to a foreign armed movement. Lebanese businessmen whom the United States designates as financiers of Hezbollah, the Lebanese Shia party and armed group, received state monopolies, including the national fuel supply and half of the state telephone companies. OCCRP, a network of investigative reporters, estimated that more than $100 million from Gambian telecoms reached Hezbollah.

For Gambians, this meant they paid for fuel and telephone calls through monopolies given to the president's associates, and some of that money left the country to fund a foreign armed group rather than reaching the treasury. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 5.

Greece.d:
Greece's documented cases show organised groups getting inside the armed forces and police, and foreign companies paying staff in the public health system. IDEA, a secret society of officers formed in 1945 by men who had served in units that worked with the German occupiers, grew inside the Greek army, and its members led the 1967 coup and held key posts under the military government that ruled until 1974.

More recently the neo-Nazi party Golden Dawn built support inside the police. After the May 2012 election, polling stations used by Attica police officers gave it just over 20 per cent of the vote against about 6 per cent at civilian stations nearby, and the Council of Europe's human rights commissioner said he had strong evidence of ties between police and the party. In 2020 its leaders were convicted of running a criminal organisation. Foreign companies reach the public health system by paying the people who choose which medicines to use, and a Swiss drug company has settled US charges of bribing Greek hospital staff and doctors; accusations against politicians were dropped.

For people in Greece, this means migrants and political opponents were policed in districts where many officers backed a party later found to be a criminal organisation, and patients were treated in public hospitals where a drug company had paid staff to prescribe its products. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 5.1.

Guinea-Bissau.d:
Since the mid-2000s Guinea-Bissau, a small West African country of islands and mangrove creeks with weak central control, has been a transit point for South American cocaine headed to Europe. The trafficking networks did not need to buy junior officials one by one, because they reached the commanders of the armed forces themselves. In 2013 US prosecutors charged the heads of the navy, the air force and the army with offering their positions to help move cocaine. The army chief, who had led a coup the year before, was also charged with offering to store cocaine for the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla army, and sell it weapons. Only the navy chief was caught, in a sting at sea; the other two stayed in Bissau and were never handed over.

The armed forces have repeatedly overthrown or threatened elected governments, so the people traffickers paid are the same people who decide who governs. The navy chief, back home after his US sentence, was blamed by the president for a failed attack on the government palace in 2022.

For people in Guinea-Bissau, this means the officers commanding their army, navy and air force have been accused of working for foreign traffickers, and those accused have remained free and in some cases in power. With the courts and watchdogs scoring under 2.7 out of 10 on the Global Organized Crime Index and officials acting for criminal interests at 8.5, the cases against them have been brought abroad, and drug cases at home rarely reach trial.

Hungary.d:
Hungary's documented cases show foreign intelligence services working through Hungarians who hold European posts. Russia's services had a Hungarian member of the European Parliament working for them: Béla Kovács, elected for the nationalist party Jobbik, was convicted in Hungary in 2022 of spying on EU institutions for Russia and lives in Russia. Hungary's own intelligence service has also used its position in Brussels to reach into EU institutions. Its officers, working under diplomatic cover at Hungary's mission to the EU, tried for years to recruit Hungarians employed at the European Commission, the EU's executive, a network the Commission has confirmed.

Both cases run through the same opening: Hungarians who hold seats or jobs in EU institutions have access to information and decisions that affect all 27 member states, which makes them worth recruiting for Moscow and for Budapest's own government. Inside Hungary, the Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 7.5 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 4.8, a weak position for an EU member.

For people in Hungary, this means a representative they elected to the European Parliament was working for a foreign intelligence service, and Hungarians working in EU institutions have been targeted by their own country's spies. When the people placed inside European bodies work for an intelligence service, decisions that affect Hungarians' rights, funds and trade are taken with a foreign or partisan service listening in.

Iran.d:
In Iran the documented reach into the state has come through religious and fraternal networks. Under the Shah, the head of Iran's main Freemason lodge served twice as prime minister. After the 1979 revolution, members of the Hojjatieh Society, a Shia religious association, sat in government and education bodies until Ayatollah Khomeini turned on the society in 1983 and they were purged; former members are reported to have later held posts in the judiciary and security services.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Iran 9.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 3 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs, among the weakest results anywhere. For people in Iran this means there is no independent court or free press able to examine which networks hold posts inside the state, or who in it profits from what.

Italy.d:
Italy's mafias get inside the state mostly at the level of the town hall. They supply votes to local politicians and in return take a say over public jobs, building contracts and permits, until a town's administration works for the clan. Since 1991 the national government has dissolved town councils and local health authorities 402 times after finding them under mafia control, mostly in Calabria, Campania and Sicily but also in Lombardy, Piedmont and Emilia-Romagna. The 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia decides who works the docks at Gioia Tauro, Italy's largest transhipment port, and its clans run construction firms in the wealthy north. Mass trials in Calabria have convicted police officers, civil servants and a former senator alongside clan members, and politicians as senior as a President of Sicily have been convicted of helping Cosa Nostra.

Secret networks have reached even further. In 1981 police seized the membership list of P2, a hidden Masonic lodge, and found it included dozens of members of parliament, serving ministers, nearly 200 senior military officers and the heads of all three intelligence services. Parliament then outlawed secret associations, and in 2017 its anti-mafia commission found 193 people in Sicilian and Calabrian lodges who appeared in mafia investigations.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Italy 7 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and above 6 for its courts and watchdogs. For people in southern Italy especially, this means their elected council can be removed and replaced by commissioners for up to two years, and public building work can go to firms a clan controls.

Kazakhstan.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Kazakhstan, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case on this map shows a foreign state, crime group, company or secret society paying or placing officials there.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kazakhstan 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 5 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. Those scores mean experts judge that some officials do act for criminal interests and that courts and press are not strong enough to expose it reliably.

For people in Kazakhstan this means the influence they are most likely to meet is the ordinary corruption and organised crime the index measures, in customs, licensing, policing and contracts. Because nothing has reached a court or an inquiry, there is no named official, company or group to point to, and residents have no public record of how far that influence goes.

Korea, Rep..d:
In South Korea, religious movements have reached the top of politics by two routes: gifts and cash to the people around power, and mass sign-ups to a party. The Unification Church, a Korean-founded movement, has worked closely with Seoul governments since the 1970s, when a US congressional inquiry found it acting as a secret envoy for the state.
