In 2026 its leader was jailed for arranging luxury gifts for the first lady and cash for a senior lawmaker of the governing People Power Party (PPP) around the 2022 presidential election, and both of them were jailed too; the church says it will appeal. Another movement, Shincheonji, signed up tens of thousands of its members to the PPP, enough to weigh on who the party picks as candidates, and its founder has been indicted.

Business reaches in through the presidency. The country's large family-run business groups depend on state decisions about mergers, licences and loans, and the head of the largest of them has been convicted of bribing a president's circle for that support, then pardoned after serving his sentence.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores South Korea 4 out of 10 for officials working for outside interests and 8 for its courts and watchdogs, among the strongest in Asia. For South Korean voters this means churches have paid their way to a first lady and a party leader and signed up enough members to sway who runs, but also that their courts have been able to expose and convict those at the top.

Laos.d:
In northern Laos a foreign-run casino company administers part of the country. In 2007 the Lao government gave Kings Romans, a company headed by the Chinese businessman Zhao Wei, a concession to set up and run the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Bokeo province, where Laos, Thailand and Myanmar meet. The US has since sanctioned his network for trafficking heroin and methamphetamine and laundering money through the zone, which he denies, and the US State Department reports that the zone is controlled and administered in part by transnational criminal organisations. No Lao official has been investigated or prosecuted for complicity.

The arrangement is how criminal networks get inside the state in Laos: rather than bribing officials one by one, they are handed land and the power to run it, under a legal concession. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Laos 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs.

For people in Laos this means land in Bokeo has been handed for decades to a company the US says moves drugs and launders money, and residents there live partly under rules set by its operators.

Liberia.d:
For most of Liberia's history, a fraternal order was part of the route to power. Membership of the Masonic Order, Liberia's Freemason body, was widely seen as a requirement for leadership in the True Whig Party, which ruled for over a century, and by the 1970s most high officials were Masons, with President William Tolbert as the order's Grand Master. Samuel Doe, who killed Tolbert in the 1980 coup, banned the order, then lifted the ban and was himself initiated while head of state.

Today the documented pressure comes from cocaine traffickers using Liberia as a stop on the route from South America to Europe. They need the airport and the police to let shipments through, and so they reach for the officials in charge of both. After the country's largest recorded seizure in 2026, nearly four tonnes bound for Europe, police charged the head of their own major crimes unit, named a senior airport security officer as a participant, and said senior government officials were involved; these are charges, not convictions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Liberia 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for its courts and watchdogs. For Liberians this means that, if the charges hold, the police unit meant to fight serious crime and the officer guarding the main airport were working with traffickers, and they cannot rely on those offices to stop drugs passing through their country.

Luxembourg.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Luxembourg, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, crime group or lodge paying officials or placing people inside its government.

The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, rates Luxembourg among the lowest in the world on that measure. That means experts judge that officials there rarely act for criminal interests.

For people living there, this means no named official or company can be shown to be acting for an outside party, and the index suggests officials face less of this pressure than in most countries. If outside money did reach in, it would most likely show up in who funds politicians, who wins public contracts and who sits on the boards of companies the state regulates, and residents are best protected when those records are public.

Maldives.d:
No case has yet been documented of a foreign state, company, religious movement or crime group with people or money inside a Maldivian ministry, court or firm, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates the Maldives in the middle range for how far officials work for criminal or outside interests, and rates its courts, police and watchdogs as fairly weak. Conditions like that usually mean some officials can be paid to serve business or criminal interests, and the bodies meant to catch them have gaps.

If the index is right, people in the Maldives would feel it as bribes asked for ordinary services, slow or uneven justice, and state contracts going to favoured firms. Without documented cases they cannot point to who benefits or which outside interests, if any, are paying. Published court records, audits of state contracts and independent reporting would be the way to find out.

Mauritania.d:
No case has yet been documented of a foreign state, company or crime group paying Mauritanian officials or placing people inside the government, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions.

Mauritania lies on the route by which South American cocaine crosses the Sahara and the Sahel towards North Africa and Europe. The UN Office on Drugs and Crime reported in 2024 that across Mauritania and its Sahel neighbours, traffickers include members of the political elite and use their profits to get into state institutions and avoid prosecution, and Mauritania itself has made some of the largest cocaine seizures in the region. The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials there often serving criminal interests and rates its courts, police and watchdogs as weak.

If the estimate is right, the pressure would show most in policing and border control, and people in Mauritania would face traffickers who are protected by officials rather than stopped by them. Without a named case there is no official or company they can yet hold to account.

Moldova.d:
Moldova's courts and elected offices have been used by outside money, most of it Russian, on a scale few countries match. The courts were used as a laundering machine: in the scheme known as the Global Laundromat, Russian companies signed fake debts that Moldovan judges ordered paid into a Moldovan bank, moving tens of billions of dollars out of Russia, and prosecutors later charged judges who approved them.

Russian money has also paid for political parties, candidates and paid protesters. Moldova's courts have banned a party for serving a foreign state's interests and jailed elected officials, including a regional governor, for funding their campaigns with undeclared Russian money.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Moldova widely serving criminal interests. For Moldovans this means a court ruling could be bought by a foreign client, and some of the people they elected, including the governor of the autonomous region of Gagauzia, owed their campaigns to a foreign government.

Morocco.d:
The documented reach into Morocco's state comes from two directions: drug traffickers who have recruited elected politicians into their networks, and a religious order whose follower holds the top post that shapes religion.

Morocco is one of the world's main producers of cannabis resin and lies on routes that carry cocaine across North Africa to Europe. Traffickers there need local officials and elected figures who can protect property, permits and shipments. The clearest case is the 'Escobar of the Sahara' network, named after a jailed Malian trafficker, in which a court in 2026 convicted a former regional council head and two former members of parliament from the governing party among dozens of defendants; appeals are open.

On the religious side, a follower of the Boutchichiya, Morocco's largest Sufi order (a Muslim brotherhood built around a spiritual teacher), has run the ministry that oversees the country's mosques since 2002, under five prime ministers. This is recorded as influence, not wrongdoing.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Morocco often serving criminal interests. For Moroccans this means that some of the people they elected to parliament and regional councils were working with a drug network rather than against it, and the ministry that shapes what is preached in their mosques has been led for more than two decades by a follower of one Sufi order.

Nauru.d:
In Nauru, a small Pacific island state whose main export is phosphate, outside money arrives mainly from Australia, and it has reached the island's politicians through the two things Australia buys there: phosphate and the hosting of asylum seekers.

Australian businesspeople seeking phosphate deals have been prosecuted in Australia for paying Nauruan politicians; one Sydney businessman was jailed in 2018 for paying an MP and a minister, and a Gold Coast phosphate trader is still awaiting trial on a charge of conspiring to bribe them. The second channel is the asylum detention centre that Australia pays contractors to run on the island. In 2023 the Sydney Morning Herald and The Age reported that subcontracts worth millions went to firms tied to Nauru's leaders, with banking records showing suspect payments to the justice minister and to a company of a man who later became president. The reporters said they were not claiming the payments were bribes, the minister denies wrongdoing, and Australia's Home Affairs department had been warned of bribery allegations for more than a decade.

In a country this small, a few contracts from one foreign government make up a large share of the money in circulation, and the politicians who decide on them can also benefit from them.

For people in Nauru this means that phosphate, one of the few sources of national income, has been sold through deals prosecutors say were bought, cutting what reaches the public. Ministers who benefit from Australian contracts have a private reason to keep the detention centre open whatever residents want.

Nicaragua.d:
In Nicaragua the documented reach into politics came from the United States in the 1980s. The National Endowment for Democracy, a foundation funded by the US Congress, paid for opposition groups and the newspaper La Prensa, and Congress added more for the opposition campaign before the 1990 election, which the opposition won. Nicaraguans who voted then were choosing between sides of which one was funded in part from Washington.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives Nicaragua one of the lowest scores in the world for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, and one of the highest for officials working for criminal or outside interests. For people in Nicaragua today, this means that if officials are working for outside interests, there is no domestic body able to examine it.

Norway.d:
Norway is one of the countries where outside forces have the least documented hold on government. The Global Organized Crime Index puts it in its minimal band, with one of the world's lowest scores for officials working for criminal interests and strong courts, police and watchdogs.

The exception the record shows is inside the police, where drug enforcement depends on officers handling informants with little outside oversight. The clearest case is Eirik Jensen, who ran the Oslo police narcotics section for years while helping an informant he managed bring around fourteen tonnes of hashish into the country, and was jailed for twenty-one years, the most senior police conviction of its kind in Scandinavia. For people in Oslo it meant that, over those years, the unit meant to stop the drug trade was protecting one of its suppliers, and drug cases it handled may have been shaped by that arrangement. It also showed the courts holding a senior officer to account through every level of appeal.

Panama.d:
Panama's place in the record comes from its role as a corridor for ships, money and companies, and from the people who have paid their way into its government because of it. Its law firms set up companies for clients abroad, its free zone in Colón lets goods pass without entering customs, and its banks have held money for traffickers and rulers alike; each of these has drawn foreign buyers of influence.

The largest recent reach came from Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group that admitted paying bribes across Latin America and Africa to win public contracts. It says it paid Panamanian officials during the 2009–2014 government, and the trial of more than 20 people, including a former president who joins by video from asylum abroad, opened in 2026. Panamanians paid for the public works on which those bribes were earned.

The pattern is older than Odebrecht. Under military rule in the 1980s, Manuel Noriega took money from Colombia's Medellín cartel for protection and made Panama a shipping platform for cocaine bound for the United States. Each time, the state's offices were rented out to whoever moved money or drugs through the corridor. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Panama high for officials working for criminal interests, and for residents it means public contracts and protection from the law have been on offer to the corridor's biggest users.

Philippines.d:
In the Philippines, outsiders reach into government through churches that deliver votes, through Chinese-run gambling businesses that bought their way into local office, and through contractors with friends close to the president.

Iglesia ni Cristo, a Philippine church of about 2.6 million members, tells its members to vote as a bloc for the candidates it chooses, which can decide close Senate races. In return its leaders receive government posts, and the church puts its members on the streets to defend officials from its own ranks when they face charges. A voter outside the church is competing with a bloc whose choices are made by its leadership.

From 2016 the government licensed Chinese-run online gambling firms serving players in China, and Senate hearings tied many of them to fraud, trafficking and the torture of workers held in their compounds. The firms secured local protection by placing allies in office; the clearest example is Alice Guo, elected mayor of Bamban in 2022 while such a hub ran in her town, later found by a court to be a Chinese citizen and sentenced to life for trafficking. Congress banned the industry in 2025.

During the pandemic, government supply contracts worth billions of pesos went to a firm with almost no capital whose suppliers were backed by a former presidential adviser, who denies formal ties. The Global Organized Crime Index scores the Philippines high for officials working for criminal interests. For Filipinos this has meant emergency money going to connected firms, and towns run by officials whose loyalty was to a gambling compound.

Romania.d:
In Romania, the documented reach into the state comes through private lodges whose membership officials do not declare.

Freemasonry, a fraternity whose members meet privately in lodges and swear mutual support, is lawful in Romania, and officials are required to list such memberships in their declarations of interests. A 2019 magazine report, based on unnamed Masonic sources, said the interim interior minister and the head of the Gendarmerie, the militarised police, belonged to lodges without declaring it; one neither confirmed nor denied, and the claim rests on that one outlet. For Romanians, it means they cannot check whether the people in charge of their police owe loyalty to a private society, because the declarations meant to show this leave it out.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Romania in the middle range both for officials working for criminal interests and for the strength of its courts and watchdogs, which suggests there is more than the record shows.

San Marino.d:
In San Marino, the documented reach into government comes from builders and bankers who paid politicians for the permits and licences they needed. In a state of about 34,000 people, a small number of politicians decide who may build and who may open a bank, and the courts have found that those decisions were bought.

In the case known as Conto Mazzini, named after an account held under the name 'Giuseppe Mazzini' at a Sammarinese bank, prosecutors showed that construction and banking entrepreneurs paid politicians, including former government ministers, with cash drawn from that account. About 200 million euros were seized, and an appeal court upheld most convictions in 2022.

For residents, it meant building permits and banking licences went to those who paid, while builders and bankers who did not pay competed against firms that had bought their approvals, and the buildings and banks approved that way are still part of daily life. It also shows the courts reaching former ministers.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores San Marino in the middle range both for officials working for criminal or outside interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs.

Serbia.d:
In Serbia the reach into the state comes mostly from Belgrade's organised crime groups, and they work through the security services rather than around them. Gangs with a share of the Balkan heroin and cocaine trade have recruited or merged with police and intelligence units, which gives them state identity cards, entry to protected buildings and warning of investigations. The clearest case came in 2003, when a commander of the interior ministry's special operations unit, which had fused with the Zemun clan, shot dead the elected prime minister, Zoran Đinđić. Prosecutors say a later gang, the Belivuk-Miljković group, again carried state security identification, and a former head of the security service has been charged in connection with it; that case is still open.

The habit of armed insiders running the state from a private organisation is older. Around the First World War, secret societies of army officers decided much of Serbian politics: the leader of one ran military intelligence, and the leader of a rival society became prime minister when the king took dictatorial power in 1929.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8 out of 10, near the top of Europe, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 4.9. For people in Serbia that means the units meant to protect them have been used by gangs, once against the government they had voted for, and they learn how far it went only through slow prosecutions that the parties fight over.

Slovakia.d:
In Slovakia outsiders have reached in through people close to the prime minister, and the public has learned of it from journalists rather than from courts. Businessmen from Calabria with suspected ties to the 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, set up farm companies in eastern Slovakia, where EU agricultural subsidies are paid, and built business links with officials in Bratislava. Journalist Ján Kuciak was finishing an article showing that the prime minister's chief adviser had co-founded a company with one of them when he and his fiancée were shot dead in 2018; the adviser stepped down, and Prime Minister Robert Fico resigned after mass protests. No court has found that the prime minister's office acted for the 'Ndrangheta.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 4.9. For Slovaks this has meant losing a reporter for exposing these links, with no court ruling on how far they reached.

South Africa.d:
South Africa's state has been run from inside by private networks twice in living memory, first a secret society and then a business family with foreign firms alongside it. Every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 belonged to the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male Afrikaner society that placed its members in top posts; by the late 1970s it held almost every cabinet seat as well as the heads of the army and the intelligence service, and the public learned the names only when two journalists printed them in 1978.

After apartheid the reach came through money. A judicial inquiry, the Zondo Commission, found that during Jacob Zuma's presidency ministers and the heads of Eskom, the state power company, and Transnet, the state rail and ports company, acted corruptly for the Gupta brothers, Indian-born businessmen who offered cabinet posts to officials willing to cooperate. Several of the world's largest consulting and engineering firms, from the United States, Switzerland and Germany, have since admitted in US settlements to bribing officials at those companies and in city councils, and the inquiry found that a US consultancy helped take over the tax service.

The reach now runs through the police and local councils. A provincial police commissioner has accused the police minister of working with a criminal syndicate, which the minister denies, and extortion groups calling themselves 'business forums' demand a share of public building contracts and pressure ward councillors. For South Africans, the bribes paid to win power and rail contracts came out of the companies that supply their electricity and move their goods, and the money was repaid only after US prosecutors stepped in.

St. Kitts and Nevis.d:
Nothing is documented yet for St Kitts and Nevis, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows an outside government, company, crime group or lodge paying Kittitian officials or placing people in office.

The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, places St Kitts and Nevis near the middle of its scale, at 5 out of 10. It gives about 5.4 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That describes officials under some pressure, with checks on them that are neither strong nor absent.

For people living there, this means no named official or company can be shown to be acting for an outside party. If outside money did reach in, it would most likely show up in who funds politicians, who wins public contracts and how licences are granted, and residents are best protected when those records are public.

Suriname.d:
In Suriname the cocaine trade did not need to buy officials from outside the government: for years it reached the presidency and the security services through the country's own leaders. Suriname lies on the Atlantic coast between Guyana and French Guiana, and the US Treasury says semi-submersible boats carry cocaine across the ocean from its ports and Guyana's.

Desi Bouterse, the former military ruler, was convicted in absentia in the Netherlands in 1999 of smuggling more than 450 kilograms of cocaine, never served the sentence because there was no extradition treaty, and was then elected president twice. While he held office his son Dino ran the country's counter-terrorism unit and used it to traffic cocaine; US agents arrested him in Panama, and he pleaded guilty in New York, including to offering a base in Suriname to people he believed were from Hezbollah, the Lebanese armed group.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8.5 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 3.2. For the Surinamese, this meant that a counter-terrorism unit paid for by their taxes was used for drug trafficking, and that a court verdict against the man they twice elected president was never enforced.

Taiwan.d:
Taiwan faces the most sustained effort on the map to reach into a democracy from outside, by China through what it calls united front work: the Chinese Communist Party's system for winning over or recruiting people abroad. It works at every level. Money from Chinese provinces and city offices has funded small parties and local council candidates, paid for trips to China for elected village chiefs, at which Chinese officials urged them how to vote, and been moved through Hong Kong accounts. Chinese military intelligence has recruited aides and retired officials, and Taiwan's courts have jailed people for passing information from close to the president and for trying to recruit soldiers.

Organised crime is one of the channels. The Chinese Unification Promotion Party, which campaigns for union with China, was founded by a former leader of the Bamboo Union, a Taiwanese organised crime gang, and legislators alleged that Chinese official money reached it through his company. The government has asked the Constitutional Court to dissolve it.

Taiwan's Anti-Infiltration Act, passed at the end of 2019, which bars taking money or instructions from China for political activity, is the basis for most of these cases, and most convictions can still be appealed. The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 4 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at 8. For Taiwanese voters this means a local candidate or village chief may have been paid or hosted by the government that claims their country, and aides with access to the president's schedule have handed it to Chinese intelligence.

Timor-Leste.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Timor-Leste, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, crime group or lodge paying officials or placing people inside its government.

Timor-Leste depends on oil and gas from the Timor Sea to fund its budget, and that kind of single, valuable source of public money is where outside interests often seek influence. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 4.5 out of 10 and the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs at about 3.9. That describes moderate pressure on officials with weak checks on them.

For people living there, this means no named official or company can be shown to be acting for an outside party. If a case exists, it would most likely surface through oil and gas deals, public contracts and policing, and those are the records residents would need to see.

Tunisia.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Tunisia, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, crime group or lodge placing people inside its government or paying its officials.

The Global Organized Crime Index puts Tunisia in its High band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 6.5 out of 10 and the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs at 4.3. That combination describes officials under real pressure and weak checks on them.

For people living there, this means that if outside interests are paying or placing officials, it is likely to show up in public contracts, customs and policing, and residents would pay through lost public revenue and weaker protection. With no named case, there is no official or company they can yet challenge.

Uganda.d:
In Uganda the clearest outside influence on lawmaking comes from American Christian networks that have worked closely with Ugandan politicians on laws against gay people. The Fellowship, a US network that organises prayer breakfasts for politicians around the world, has a Ugandan chapter chaired by David Bahati, who first floated his 2009 bill proposing the death penalty for homosexuality at a Uganda prayer breakfast and has been a government minister since 2021. When Uganda passed the Anti-Homosexuality Act in 2023, with life imprisonment and in some cases death, a Ugandan activist named the president of Family Watch International, an Arizona-based Christian lobbying group, as one of those who had lobbied for it.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Uganda at 8 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 3.7, which leaves little independent scrutiny of who is influencing ministers and MPs.

For gay Ugandans, the effect is a law that can send them to prison for life, backed by lobbyists from abroad. The World Bank halted new lending to Uganda in August 2023 because of the law, so funding for public projects that every Ugandan uses was cut over a measure that foreign campaigners helped push and that most of those affected had no part in.

United States.d:
In the United States the most common way outside interests get inside government is legal and open: they write the laws and staff the offices. Groups funded largely by industry, led by the American Legislative Exchange Council, where companies and state legislators draft 'model bills' together, produced at least 10,000 bills introduced in state legislatures between 2010 and 2018, of which more than 2,100 became law. Think tanks and lawyers' networks on both sides of politics prepare the people who staff whole administrations and fill the federal appeals courts. Senior Goldman Sachs bankers have repeatedly moved into the Treasury and White House posts that oversee their old firm.

Where the influence turns into bribery, it is often a utility or contractor buying a state legislature's leader; in Ohio, FirstEnergy paid about $60 million to a group around the House Speaker for a law rescuing its nuclear plants. Foreign governments work through members of Congress, local officials and aides; courts have convicted people acting for Egypt, China, Cuba and Saudi Arabia. North Korea has placed its programmers in hundreds of US companies under false identities, and Mexican cartels pay border officers to let loads through, producing more than 200 corruption convictions in a decade.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 4.5 out of 10. For Americans, the cost shows up in bills and rules: Ohio households pay electricity prices set by a law that was bought, and many state laws were drafted by the industries they regulate.

Vatican City.d:
The Vatican is both the centre of the Catholic Church and a sovereign state, with its own bank, the Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR), and its own courts that answer to the Pope. Its exposure to outside interests comes through money: financiers and middlemen who handle the Holy See's funds can use its sovereignty as a shield, because Italian courts cannot reach inside.

The case whose effect is still felt is the collapse of Banco Ambrosiano, a Milan bank, in 1982. The IOR was its main shareholder and was tied to the offshore companies that held the missing money, and Ambrosiano's chairman belonged to P2, a secret Masonic lodge that had enrolled Italian intelligence chiefs and politicians. The IOR denied liability but paid creditors $224 million in 1984. When Milan magistrates sought to arrest the IOR's president, Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, in 1987, Italy's top court ruled that the 1929 Lateran Treaty shielded the bank's central bodies, and he stayed inside the Vatican and was never tried.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7 out of 10. For Catholics who give money to the Church, and for the creditors and savers of banks the Vatican deals with, this means that losses caused through the IOR can fall outside the reach of ordinary courts. Any case against Vatican officials is heard by judges appointed by the Pope, so those who were harmed have to rely on the Holy See to investigate itself.

Zambia.d:
Zambia's 1996 constitution declares it a Christian nation, and the pattern recorded here is organised religion moving into the machinery of government. Pentecostal and evangelical church networks, some of them founded abroad, are active in Zambian public life, and under President Edgar Lungu the state gave them a ministry of their own. In 2016 Lungu turned a religious-affairs desk into a full Ministry of National Guidance and Religious Affairs and appointed a cleric, Rev. Godfridah Sumaili, as a nominated MP so she could run it; she held the post for five years. After the 2021 election President Hakainde Hichilema folded the ministry into a department of the Vice-President's office.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Zambia in its Moderate band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 6.5 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 4.7. No case is documented of a foreign state or company placing people inside the Zambian government.

For Zambians, the effect of the religious ministry was that one faith had a minister in the cabinet and a budget line to promote its values, while Zambians of other faiths, or none, had no equivalent voice in government. The ministry was created by the president, not through a public vote, and was dissolved the same way, so the place of religion in the state depends on who holds the presidency.

Andorra.d:
Andorra is a small mountain state between France and Spain whose economy has long relied on private banking for foreign clients. That makes its banks the obvious place for outside money to try to get in, and the documented pattern here is crime-group money handled by bank insiders rather than by politicians.

The case on the map is Banca Privada d'Andorra, whose senior managers, the US Treasury found in 2015, knowingly moved money for professional launderers working for transnational criminal organisations. Andorra took the bank over the next day and wound it up within a week. The US later withdrew its finding, but an Andorran court sentenced eighteen of the bank's executives in 2025; they are appealing, and shareholders argue the bank was closed on an administrative finding never tested in court.

Outside banking there is little on record. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Andorra 1 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests, the lowest possible score, and 8 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, the cost of the bank case fell on its ordinary clients, who had to prove their money was legitimate before they could get it back, some waiting years, while the country's standing as a banking centre, which much of its income depends on, was put in question.

Armenia.d:
No case of an outside government, company, crime group or secret society placing people or money inside Armenia's government or companies remains on this map after checking. That is a statement about the documented record, not proof that none exists.

What the wider evidence shows is a country where this kind of reach-in is rated as a modest problem. The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, gives Armenia 3.5 out of 10 on that measure, low by world standards. It gives Armenia about 5.6 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, which is around the middle of the range.

For people living in Armenia, this means there is no documented case in which they can point to an outside party steering a ministry, court or company against them. The scores suggest the main protection is that institutions are rated as working moderately well, and that officials are not widely judged to answer to criminal interests. Where outside influence does exist, it is most likely to show up in who wins public contracts, who owns the companies that run essential services and who funds political campaigns, and those are the records residents would need to see in order to spot it early.

Bahamas.d:
No case of an outside government, company, crime group or secret society placing people or money inside the government or companies of the Bahamas remains on this map after checking. That is a statement about the documented record, not proof that none exists.

The Bahamas is an offshore financial centre, where foreign banks and companies register to hold money for clients abroad, and it sits on sea routes between South America and the United States. Both features are the kind that draw outside money looking for protection. Against that, the Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, gives the Bahamas 3 out of 10 on that measure, low by world standards, and about 5.6 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, around the middle of the range.

For people living in the Bahamas, this means there is no documented case in which they can point to a foreign bank, cartel or government steering a ministry, regulator or court against them. If outside money were reaching in, it would most likely show up in the supervision of offshore banks, in policing of the islands' coasts and in who owns registered companies, which are the records residents would need to be able to see.

Belarus.d:
No case of an outside party placing people or money inside Belarus's government or companies remains on this map after checking, so the picture here rests on how the country is rated rather than on documented incidents.

Belarus has been ruled by Alexander Lukashenko since 1994, and power is concentrated around the presidency and the security services. The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, gives Belarus 9 out of 10 on that measure, among the highest in Europe. It gives about 3.1 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, which is among the lowest. Taken together, those scores describe a state in which officials are judged to act widely for interests other than the public's and in which no independent body is able to check them.

For people living in Belarus, this means that if an outside government, company or criminal group did get people inside a ministry or state firm, there would be no free press, independent court or opposition party able to expose it. The absence of a documented case here reflects how little can be investigated in the country as much as anything else, and residents have no independent channel to raise it themselves.

Bhutan.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Bhutan, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No foreign intelligence service, company, crime group, church or lodge has a documented presence in its government or companies, and none is listed as likely to be present.

Bhutan is a small Himalayan kingdom between India and China, which limits foreign investment and tourism, and it became a parliamentary democracy only in 2008. The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, gives Bhutan 3 out of 10 on that measure, low by world standards, and about 4.7 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. The estimate rests on that index alone.

For people living there, this means no known cost from outside groups placing people in Bhutan's offices or firms, and the index rates this as a smaller problem than in most of the world. The middling resilience score means that if outside influence did arrive, through its large neighbours or through investment, the institutions that would have to catch it are not rated as especially strong. A documented case found later would replace this estimate.

Brazil.d:
Brazil has more documented cases of outsiders inside its institutions than almost any country on this map, and they come from three directions: organised crime, churches and companies.

The largest criminal group, the PCC (Primeiro Comando da Capital), began in São Paulo's prisons and now runs much of the drug trade. Prosecutors say it has owned bus companies running city routes on public contracts, paid civil police officers to shield its members, and, through dozens of investment funds, held ethanol plants, a port terminal and more than a thousand petrol stations, where drivers were sold fuel cut with illegal methanol. In Rio de Janeiro, militias, armed groups that began as off-duty police running protection rackets, tax residents in the areas they control and have allies in elected office; Brazil's top court found in 2026 that a federal deputy and his brother ordered the 2018 killing of councillor Marielle Franco over militia land interests.

Churches have built their own power inside the state. Pastors of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God founded the Republicanos party, which a church bishop leads, and the cross-party evangelical caucus lists 213 of the 513 federal deputies. Companies reach in through Congress and state firms: the farm caucus's agenda is drafted by an institute funded by agribusiness and pesticide companies, and construction firms and commodity traders have paid officials of the state oil company, Petrobras, for contracts.

For people living there, this means bus fares and petrol purchases can feed a crime group, residents of militia areas pay protection to groups tied to their own representatives, and laws on pesticides, land and religion are often written by those with a direct stake in them.

Burundi.d:
In Burundi the documented reach comes from a foreign tobacco company working on the officials who write tobacco law. Leaked records from British American Tobacco (BAT), one of the world's largest cigarette makers, show payments to Burundian officials who handled tobacco control, part of a run of such payments in several East and Central African countries that researchers read as aimed at blocking laws modelled on the WHO tobacco treaty, which commits governments to restrict tobacco sales and marketing. A British fraud inquiry closed without charges and BAT denies the allegations, so these remain reports rather than findings.

If the payments worked as the records suggest, Burundians live under weaker tobacco rules than the treaty asks for: more advertising, cheaper and easier access, fewer health warnings, and over time more illness from smoking. No Burundian inquiry is recorded, so residents do not know which officials were paid or what they did in return.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Burundi among the countries where officials most often work for criminal interests, and its courts, police and watchdogs among the weakest. On those terms, an official who takes money from a foreign company is unlikely to be investigated at home, which is why the only account of these payments came from a British broadcaster and a British university.

Canada.d:
Most of what reaches inside Canadian government today comes from foreign states working through their own diaspora communities and through proxies. China and India are the most active: Canada's public inquiry into foreign interference found intelligence that India's proxy agents may have given illicit money to Canadian politicians to elect pro-India candidates, and a parliamentary intelligence committee reported that some MPs and senators had knowingly or half-knowingly helped foreign states, including by taking disguised money from foreign missions. The inquiry found no traitors in Parliament, but for voters it means a candidate on the ballot may have had a foreign government's help getting there.

Organised crime and companies reach in where public money and goods change hands. In Montreal, construction firms paid the Mafia a share of city public works contracts and also paid political parties, and at the busiest land crossings into the United States, border officers have been convicted of waving smugglers' vehicles through.

Earlier, membership did the work. For the first half of the 20th century Toronto's city hall was run by members of the Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity: every mayor in that period belonged to it, as did four prime ministers. Canada's courts, police and watchdogs are among the strongest measured by the Global Organized Crime Index, which is why most of these cases came to light through Canada's own inquiries.

China.d:
In China the reaching-in mostly runs the other way: the Communist Party places its own bodies inside companies, foreign ones included. The law requires any firm with three or more party members to set up a party organisation, and by the party's own count nearly three-quarters of private companies had one by 2018. Chinese state partners in foreign joint ventures have asked the foreign side to write party groups into company rules, and the party has told its United Front departments, which manage its relations with groups outside the party, to 'guide' private firms.

Foreign companies have reached in through officials' families and through public health bodies. JPMorgan hired about a hundred relatives and friends of officials and state-company executives to win business, and an industry-funded science group founded by a Coca-Cola executive had its China office inside the national disease control agency, where researchers found it steered obesity policy towards exercise rather than diet and sugary drinks.

Organised crime has bought local police and party officials in some cities and villages, from deputy police chiefs to village party secretaries shielding drug labs, and the party has answered with campaigns of mass arrests and executions. For people in China, this means working alongside party bodies the law requires, public health advice shaped by food makers' money, and in some places police who protected the gangs. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Chinese officials high for working with criminal interests, with institutions of middling strength.

Congo, Rep..d:
What is documented for the Republic of Congo is a Masonic network that runs from the presidency to France and into a neighbouring country. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges, swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites; a national grand lodge is headed by a grand master. Press reports say President Denis Sassou-Nguesso is Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Congo-Brazzaville, which is linked to a French Masonic body, the Grande Loge Nationale Française, and that he sponsored the initiation of the Central African Republic's president. An earlier Congolese president was reported to have been initiated in a lodge in France.

So the man at the head of the government also heads the lodge network at home, and that network connects him to French Freemasonry and to a neighbouring head of state. These are press reports, lodge membership is lawful, and the reporting does not show any decision taken for a lodge. What it means for Congolese is that their president, his officials and foreign contacts can meet in a setting that voters, journalists and courts cannot see into.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country among those where officials most often work for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs, so little inside the country would check such ties if they were used.

Cuba.d:
Cuba is a one-party state whose own intelligence and security services control most of public life, and the documented case of outside reach runs against that grain: a foreign cartel bought officers of the state. In 1989 General Arnaldo Ochoa, a decorated army commander, and an Interior Ministry colonel who ran the state's hard-currency businesses were convicted of letting the Medellín cartel move cocaine to Florida through Cuban waters and airspace, and both were executed by firing squad.

The case showed that a Colombian cartel could reach senior officers inside a state that tightly controls its own territory, and that those officers used state channels to do it. The punishment was public and severe, but it was carried out by military courts that Cubans have no independent way to check, so the public record of how far the network reached is the one the government chose to give.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cuba's officials as relatively unlikely to work for criminal interests, with institutions of middling strength. No more recent case on the map shows a foreign state, company or criminal group placing people inside the Cuban government, though the closed nature of the state means little would be reported if one did.

Djibouti.d:
Djibouti's documented case is a foreign company paying the state's own officials for a state contract. Ericsson, the Swedish telecoms equipment maker, admitted paying about €2.1 million to high-ranking Djibouti officials to win a contract with Djibouti Telecom, the state-owned telephone company, as part of a US settlement covering bribery in several countries. The payment went to the people inside the state who decide which foreign supplier builds a national network, so the contract was settled by the bribe rather than by price or quality.

For Djiboutians, the telephone network they pay for was built under a contract won by bribing their officials, and they learned of it from a US settlement rather than from any process at home. The officials who took the money were not named in public, and no case against them in Djibouti is recorded.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Djibouti in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs. The Ericsson payments are the only case on record.

Egypt.d:
In Egypt the outside force that came closest to the top of the state is the Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928 that works to bring its members into power. In June 2012 one of its senior figures, Mohamed Morsi, won the presidential election as the candidate of the Brotherhood's own party, so for one year a member of the movement held the highest office. The army removed him in July 2013, most of the Brotherhood's leaders were jailed in the following months, and the government declared it a terrorist organisation. Membership alone can now bring a prison sentence.

The other lasting pattern is control by creditors. After Egypt's ruler went bankrupt in 1876, Britain and France put their own controllers over its finances to make sure European lenders were paid. The British controller, Evelyn Baring, came from the family whose bank held Egyptian debt, and from 1883 to 1907 he effectively ruled the country while keeping its revenues committed to those creditors.

For Egyptians the result is a state that treats an organised religious-political movement as an enemy within, and a political system where people who voted for the Brotherhood saw their president removed by the army and their party outlawed. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 8.5 out of 10 and the strength of the courts and watchdogs at 3.75, so there is little independent check on how the state itself uses its power.

Estonia.d:
Estonia's documented exposure comes through its banks. Because Tallinn's banks sit inside the European Union but next to Russia and the former Soviet states, money from those countries has used them as a gateway into Europe. The clearest case is the Azerbaijani Laundromat: leaked records published in 2017 showed about $2.9 billion moved in 2012–2014 through UK shell companies with accounts at Danske Bank's Estonian branch, almost half of it from an account linked to the family that rules Azerbaijan. Part of that money reached European politicians, including members who defended Azerbaijan in the Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly, the body that monitors elections and human rights across 46 countries.

The other thread is the elite networks that recruit rising politicians. Economy minister Erkki Keldo joined the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders in 2025, a programme in which the Swiss foundation behind the Davos meeting picks people under about 40 for five years of meetings with business and government figures. Membership is lawful, and no finding says it steered his decisions.

For Estonians, the banking case meant their financial system was used to pay politicians elsewhere in Europe to speak for a foreign ruling family, which damaged the reputation of the banks they depend on. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Estonian officials acting for criminal interests at 2 out of 10 and its courts and watchdogs at above 8, among the strongest in the world, so the risk here lies in the money passing through rather than in officials being bought at home.

Finland.d:
Finland has one of the cleanest records on the map. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 1.5 out of 10 and the strength of its courts and watchdogs at over 8.4, among the highest in the world, and no case shows a foreign state, company or criminal group paying Finnish officials.

What is documented is the reach of private elite networks into the country's top offices. The World Economic Forum, the Swiss foundation behind the annual Davos meeting, picks rising politicians under about 40 for its Young Global Leaders network, which brings them together with business executives over several years. Finland's president, Alexander Stubb, joined it in 2009 and lists it on his official CV, and former prime minister Sanna Marin is also listed as a member. Membership is lawful and public, and no finding says the network directed Finnish government decisions.

For people in Finland this means their head of state and a recent head of government were chosen early in their careers for a network funded by large companies, whose meetings are not public. Finns can see that they belong but not what is discussed there. With strong courts and a free press, the main question is about whose views leaders hear before they take decisions, rather than about bribery.

Georgia.d:
In Georgia the best-documented force that has reached into the state is the 'thieves in law', a criminal fraternity born in Soviet prison camps in the 1930s whose members swear to live by its code and settle disputes for others. Through the 1990s, after independence, Georgian governments treated them as part of the country's power structure rather than as criminals, according to Georgian analysts and former officials.

In 2005 Georgia passed a law that made membership of the fraternity a crime in itself, and the European Court of Human Rights later upheld it. The fraternity has not disappeared: in late 2025 and early 2026 police arrested more than 100 people in a nationwide crackdown on its networks, including suspected thieves in law, though its leaders mostly direct things from abroad or from prison.

For Georgians this means a criminal network that once operated alongside the state is still active in their communities, and arrests tend to reach low-level members rather than those in charge. No case on the map shows a foreign government or company currently placing or paying officials in Georgia. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 4 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at 5, a middle position.

Grenada.d:
Grenada has given ambassador titles to foreign businessmen, and the documented allegations here come from foreign investors dealing directly with the prime minister's office. In 2019 an Al Jazeera investigation reported that one foreign investor said he had paid about half a million dollars to Prime Minister Keith Mitchell, who said he received only $15,000 to cover travel. A US businessman said a partner had been offered a diplomatic post in return for kickbacks on state projects, which the government denies. No charge has been brought, and the claims rest on the investors' own statements.

For Grenadians, this means public contracts and diplomatic posts can be traded with foreign investors, and only the government's word stands between residents and that trade. If a kickback was asked for, it raised the cost of work done for the public. With no court test, residents are left with conflicting accounts. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 3.5 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 5.2, better than most of the region.

Guyana.d:
Guyana produces gold in its interior and has become a route for cocaine moving from South America by air and sea, and the people in both trades pay officials to keep their business moving. According to the US Treasury, the largest gold trading family in the country bribed customs officials to leave more than 10,000 kilograms of gold off customs declarations, paid officials for help in court matters and to win state contracts, and was helped by the top civil servant at the home affairs ministry, who took cash and gifts for contracts, gun permits and passports. The family denies wrongdoing.

Cocaine networks reach the police in the same way. In 2025 the Treasury sanctioned a serving police officer it says arranged safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan traffickers, along with men it says run the largest trafficking organisations in the country and Colombians managing hidden airstrips in the jungle, often in the Barima-Waini region in the north-west. None of these cases has been tried, and the US State Department calls corruption in Guyana a significant obstacle to stopping drugs.

For Guyanese, this means the customs officer, court official or ministry clerk they deal with for a permit or passport may have been paid by a large private business, and duty lost on undeclared gold, more than $50 million by the Treasury's count, was public money. People in the interior live near airstrips used for cocaine, policed by a force that traffickers have reached. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 4.3.

Iceland.d:
No case has been documented of a foreign government, criminal group, company or secret society placing people or money inside Iceland's government, so this account is an estimate built from the conditions there rather than from a record.

Those conditions point to a low risk. The Global Organized Crime Index, which rates every country from 1 to 10, puts Iceland among the lowest anywhere for officials working for criminal interests and near the top for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. The Mont Pelerin Society, a private club of free-market economists and politicians, has members in the country, but membership is lawful and nothing on record shows it steering a decision.

For people in Iceland this means they are unlikely to meet an official quietly serving a foreign state or a crime group when they apply for a licence, go to court or report a crime. It also means that any outside influence that does exist has never been tested by a court or an inquiry, so residents have no public record to judge its size by.

Iraq.d:
Iraq pays for armed groups that answer to another country. The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) formed in 2014 to fight Islamic State and are made up of about 67 mostly Shia militias, almost all backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards. A 2016 law made them a branch of Iraq's armed forces, under the prime minister and paid from the state budget, and their own chief of staff has said publicly that the force takes orders from Iran's supreme leader. Militias the US lists as terrorist groups staff some PMF brigades, and the PMF's chairman, who has also been national security adviser, has kept his post despite US sanctions over the killing of protesters.

Criminal networks have reached the top of the civil service as well, mostly through the offices that hold and pay out public money. In the clearest case, about $2.5 billion was taken from a tax commission account in 2021 and 2022 through fake refunds to front companies, with the director of the prime minister's office among those later convicted.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Iraq 8.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3 for its courts and watchdogs. For Iraqis this means their taxes fund militias whose leaders say they follow a foreign cleric and whose actions have drawn US strikes onto Iraqi soil, while money owed to the treasury can be taken by people working beside the head of government.

Jamaica.d:
In parts of Kingston, Jamaica's political parties and armed gangs have depended on each other for decades. In 'garrison' neighbourhoods, each loyal to one party, a local gang leader known as a 'don' delivers votes and keeps order, and in return receives public contracts and protection from the state. The arrangement is how a criminal organisation gets inside government in Jamaica: not by buying a single official, but by becoming part of how a constituency is run.

The clearest case is the Shower Posse, whose leader Christopher Coke ran Tivoli Gardens, a West Kingston neighbourhood in the prime minister's own constituency. When the United States asked for his extradition, the government resisted for nine months and hired a Washington law firm to lobby against it; the police and army operation that finally went in to take him in 2010 killed at least 69 people, and the prime minister resigned over the affair.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Jamaica 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and just over 5 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For people living in garrison neighbourhoods this means the person who controls their streets may be shielded by the party they are expected to vote for, and when the state does move against him, residents are the ones caught in the fighting. An official inquiry found the Tivoli operation unjustified in how it was carried out, but no inquiry has measured how far gang ties still reach into Jamaican politics.

Kenya.d:
In Kenya, drug traffickers moving heroin through the port of Mombasa have bought protection from the state at every level they needed: police to look away, prosecutors and judges to stall cases, and officials with a say over the port itself. The clearest proof came from the traffickers: the Akasha brothers, who ran a Mombasa heroin business, admitted in a US court that they had paid Kenyan judges, prosecutors and police for two years to block their extradition, and none of those officials has been named or charged in Kenya. The United States has also named a sitting MP who, as assistant transport minister, oversaw the Ports Authority as a drug kingpin; he denies it and a disputed police inquiry cleared him.

A different kind of tie ran through the central bank, which was governed from 2015 to 2023 by a celibate 'numerary' member of Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation; membership is lawful and no record shows the organisation directing his decisions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kenya 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and just over 5 for its courts and watchdogs. For Kenyans this means that some of the judges, prosecutors and police they rely on have taken trafficking money and have still not been identified, and that what is known came out in a foreign court through the traffickers' own confessions.

Kosovo.d:
In Kosovo, the documented concern is that the state's own founding generation has been accused of running criminal trades from inside government. A 2010 Council of Europe report said a group of former Kosovo Liberation Army commanders, led by the then prime minister Hashim Thaçi, controlled trades including heroin; Thaçi denied it, and while he is now on trial for war crimes, the organised-crime claims have never been tested in court.

The Global Organized Crime Index does not score Kosovo separately; North Macedonia's figures, 6.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and just over 5 for courts and watchdogs, stand in for it here. For people in Kosovo this means the claim that a former prime minister's circle profited from heroin is still unanswered by any court.

Latvia.d:
In Latvia, Russia's security services have sought influence through the parties that speak for the country's large Russian-speaking minority. Those parties give Moscow a natural route into Latvian and European politics, and the one documented case shows how far it can reach. Leaked emails published in 2024 show Tatjana Ždanoka, who represented Latvia in the European Parliament for twenty years and co-led the Latvian Russian Union party, reporting to officers of the FSB, Russia's main security and intelligence service, from at least 2004. Latvia's security service has opened a criminal case and the European Parliament penalised her, but she has not been convicted.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Latvia 2.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and above 7.5 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For people in Latvia this means that for two decades one of the people they sent to make European law was, on the evidence of her own emails, reporting to a foreign intelligence service. With the criminal case still open, voters do not yet have a court's finding on what she passed on.

Libya.d:
Libya is split between a government in Tripoli and the forces of Khalifa Haftar in the east, and on both sides armed groups have taken over the state bodies that are meant to police them. Smuggling networks have their own people in coast guard units, ports and the fuel distribution system, so that the officials who should stop fuel, migrants and drugs leaving the country are the ones moving them. The clearest case is Zawiya, a port in western Libya, where the UN sanctioned the serving coast guard commander in 2018 for fuel smuggling, migrant trafficking and violence at sea; he was released without conviction. Libya sells petrol at home for about 3 US cents a litre, and the investigative group The Sentry estimates that about $20 billion worth of subsidised fuel was diverted between 2022 and 2024, with networks tied to leaders in both east and west taking a share.

The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement, reached the top of the Tripoli government through its political arm, whose member chaired the High Council of State, the government's upper consultative body, from 2018 to 2023.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Libya 9.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 2 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs, among the worst in the world. For Libyans this means they pay for a fuel subsidy that is resold abroad for private profit, and migrants picked up at sea can find themselves in the hands of a coast guard run by the people trafficking them.

Madagascar.d:
Madagascar's documented outside reach comes through elections, from a foreign network that courts several candidates at once. In the 2018 presidential race, political strategists tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, the businessman behind the Russian private military company Wagner, worked with as many as eight candidates, offering cash or promises of money, according to the Russian outlet Proekt and the BBC; the winner denied being Russia's candidate and no evidence showed he took Russian money.

This is the approach Prigozhin's network used across much of Africa: back several contenders, so that whoever wins may owe something. In Madagascar it met a state that the Global Organized Crime Index rates as highly exposed, with officials often serving criminal or outside interests and weak courts, police and watchdogs to check them.

That weakness is why no Malagasy court or official inquiry has set out who took money or what was promised in return. For Malagasy voters it means they chose a president in a race where a foreign network was paying or courting candidates, and they have no official record of which of the people they elected, if any, owe that network anything.

Mali.d:
In Mali, the outside forces that reach into the state are mostly cocaine traffickers crossing the Sahara and the Sahel, the dry belt south of it, together with the armed groups and officials who protect them. South American cocaine moves through the region on its way to Europe. Where the routes cross desert airstrips and border posts, traffickers pay local officials and armed groups to let the cargo through, and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime has found that the traffickers include members of the political elite and armed-group leaders, and that the profits go into gold and property. The clearest single example is the 2009 'Air Cocaine' flight, when a Boeing 727 from Venezuela unloaded at a desert strip in the north and was burned, under protection that investigators traced to local officials and armed groups; no senior figure was ever convicted.

There is also an older report, from the magazine Jeune Afrique in 2012, that the president of the time oversaw Mali's national body of Freemasonry, a fraternal society whose members meet privately. It does not show any decision taken for the lodge.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Mali's courts, police and watchdogs among the weakest in the world and finds officials widely serving criminal interests. For people in Mali this means that traffickers and the officials who shelter them are rarely brought to court, and that drug money pays armed groups fighting in the areas where they live.

Mauritius.d:
The documented outside reach into Mauritius runs through state contracts, where foreign builders bidding for public infrastructure have paid officials to win the work. The clearest case concerns the Saint-Louis power station of the state electricity company: the African Development Bank, which lends for such projects, found that a Danish power-plant builder had more likely than not paid members of the Mauritian administration through middlemen during the tenders, and barred the firm from bidding on its projects for nearly two years. That is a lender's decision, not a court verdict, and it names no Mauritian official.

Paying through middlemen is the usual way this is done in public tenders: the money passes through agents or consultants, so the official who decides the contract never appears on the company's books. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a moderate level of officials serving outside interests in Mauritius and rates its institutions in the middle range.

For Mauritians this means part of the electricity they pay for comes from a station whose builder was found to have paid officials to win the work. Because the finding came from a foreign lender's internal process rather than a Mauritian court, no official has been named, and people do not know whether those involved in the tender are still in the public service.

Monaco.d:
The cases that touch Monaco come from the international bodies and wealthy foreign residents who base themselves there. The principality hosts sports federations and some of the world's richest people, and the documented problems arise where their money meets the decisions made in Monaco.

The clearest case is World Athletics, the governing body of track and field, which has its headquarters in Monaco. Its former president, Lamine Diack, was convicted in France of taking money from Russian sports officials to delay doping cases against Russian athletes, so that suspected dopers could compete at the 2012 London Olympics. In the second case, Dmitry Rybolovlev, a Russian billionaire who owns the AS Monaco football club, was suspected of courting Monaco officials, including a former public prosecutor; the case was closed after the courts ruled that the phone messages it rested on had been obtained unlawfully, so no court has decided whether officials were influenced.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds a fairly low level of officials serving outside interests in Monaco. For people there, the athletics case shows a body run from their city selling decisions to a foreign state, at the expense of athletes everywhere who competed clean. The Rybolovlev case leaves residents with no finding either way on whether a wealthy resident could buy favour from their prosecutors.

Mozambique.d:
Mozambique has been reached from outside by foreign lenders and contractors who paid its officials, and by drug traffickers who have worked alongside the ruling party for decades.

The clearest case is the 'hidden debts'. Foreign banks, including Credit Suisse and Russia's VTB, lent about 2 billion dollars to three state companies for fishing and maritime security projects with Privinvest, an Emirati-Lebanese shipbuilder, under state guarantees kept from parliament and the International Monetary Fund. US prosecutors said hundreds of millions went in bribes and kickbacks to bankers and Mozambican officials, the former finance minister was convicted in the United States, and Mozambique's own constitutional council declared the loans void. The arrangement depended on a few officials signing guarantees in the state's name without telling the bodies meant to approve them.

Traffickers have used the country as a heroin route for about thirty years. Research for the Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime in 2018 described what its authors called tight integration between traffickers and ruling-party figures, pointing to almost no heroin seizures in all that time, and a businessman designated as a trafficker abroad has remained prominent at home without charge.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Mozambique serving criminal interests to one of the highest degrees anywhere. For Mozambicans the hidden loans meant debt their parliament never approved. When the loans came to light in 2016, the IMF and World Bank froze support, and one study estimated that two million people were pushed into poverty.

Nepal.d:
The documented outside reach into Nepal's politics came from China, and it worked through the ruling party rather than through money. Nepal lies between China and India, and both have long tried to influence which leaders and parties govern in Kathmandu. When members of the governing Nepal Communist Party revolted against their own leader, Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli, in 2020, China's ambassador held a series of meetings with Oli, the president and senior party leaders, and Nepali media reported that she urged them to keep the party united. Later that year Beijing sent a delegation from the Chinese Communist Party's International Department, the office that manages its ties with foreign parties, to meet the same leaders. Former ministers and diplomats called this interference; the Chinese embassy said it only wished to see the party united.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Nepal widely serving criminal or outside interests and rates its institutions as weak.

For Nepali voters this means that a split inside the party they elected, which would decide who led the government, was discussed with a foreign ambassador and a foreign party delegation while the public was still learning of it.

Niger.d:
Niger lies on a Sahel route that the UN drugs office describes as a natural stopover for South American cocaine heading to Europe. Where a trafficking route crosses a thinly policed country, traffickers make use of local officials, whose vehicles and offices are less likely to be searched; the clearest example is a mayor caught in early 2022 with more than 200 kilograms of cocaine in his vehicle, with no outcome recorded since. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Niger high for officials working for criminal interests and low for the strength of its courts and police, so residents have little reason to expect a trial that shows who else was involved.

An older thread runs through the presidency. Press reports have named a former president, like several heads of state in former French West and Central Africa, as a Freemason, a member of a fraternity whose members swear mutual support, though no official finding confirms it.

Oman.d:
Nothing documented yet shows a foreign state, company, crime group or secret society with people or money inside Omani offices or firms, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions. Two outside bodies have been suggested as present at one time, the collapsed bank BCCI and the private political club Le Cercle, but no source documents either.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Oman in its moderate band, scoring it in the middle range both for officials working for criminal or outside interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. Read together, those scores suggest that outside interests have some room to reach officials and that the bodies which would expose them are of middling strength.

For residents, the practical meaning is that they cannot see whether contracts go to favoured firms or whether crimes linked to officials go unpunished. Published court records, audits and lists of who owns the companies doing business with the state would be the first places such a pattern would show.

Papua New Guinea.d:
In Papua New Guinea, outsiders have reached officials through contracts paid for by Australia and through police who let drug flights land.

Australia's offshore asylum centre on Manus Island brought large contracts paid in Australian dollars into a country where officials decide on visas, land and permits, and a former contractor executive has alleged that some of that money reached a businessman close to senior officials, an allegation that is denied and untested. Drug traffickers using PNG as a route to Australia have relied on police help: after a plane carrying 548 kilograms of cocaine crashed near Port Moresby in 2020, the police commissioner said there are criminals in uniform in the constabulary, yet the officers alleged to have helped were not charged.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores PNG among the highest in the world for officials working for criminal interests and low for the strength of its courts and police, so residents have little reason to trust the force to police itself.

Poland.d:
In Poland, the clearest case of an outside body placing its people inside the state comes from a domestic religious-legal movement rather than a foreign power. Ordo Iuris, a conservative Catholic legal institute that drafts laws and campaigns to change policy, saw its co-founder, Aleksander Stępkowski, made deputy foreign minister by the Law and Justice government in 2015 and then appointed to the Supreme Court with no prior experience as a judge, through an appointments council whose overhaul was contested, before he was made acting head of the court in 2020.

For Poles, this meant that the court of final appeal was led for a time by the founder of an organisation that writes the laws it then wants upheld, and that the near-total abortion ban put before parliament in 2016 came from the same institute.

The foreign reach documented in Poland runs through telecoms. Prosecutors say Chinese intelligence worked through a senior Huawei employee and a former officer of Poland's own security service to win contracts giving insight into state and local government data systems. Both deny it, and the trial has been held behind closed doors, so residents cannot follow what the evidence shows about who had access to public data.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Poland in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests.

Russia.d:
