In Russia the reach usually runs the other way from most countries on this map: the state's own security services reach into business, sport and local government, and into other countries, rather than outsiders reaching into the Russian state.

At home, the FSB, Russia's security service, and the officials around the president use arrests, decrees and friendly banks to move companies into the hands of people they trust. Business owners in disputes with someone well connected can find themselves arrested by the FSB on fraud charges, including foreign investors. For Russians who own or work for a business, this means a company can be lost through an arrest, not a court case they could win.

The same services reach into institutions that are meant to be independent. Reports for the World Anti-Doping Agency found that the sports ministry and the FSB ran a state system to hide doped athletes through the Moscow testing laboratory, protecting more than 1,000 Russian competitors between 2011 and 2015 and leaving athletes elsewhere competing against them unfairly. In the regions, criminal gangs have operated for years with protection from local police and officials, which came to light in Kushchyovskaya only after a gang murdered 12 people there in 2010.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives Russia one of the highest scores in the world for officials working for criminal interests and low marks for the strength of its courts and watchdogs.

Sao Tome and Principe.d:
Nothing is documented yet for São Tomé and Príncipe, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions. No case shows an outside government, company, crime group or lodge paying officials or placing people in office here. The only outside organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order that has diplomatic relations with many states and runs medical and aid work; its presence is lawful and is not evidence of wrongdoing.

The Global Organized Crime Index places the country in its low band, scoring it low for officials working for criminal or outside interests, though the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs is also below the middle of the scale. That combination suggests less outside pressure than in many states, but also fewer bodies able to find it if it were there.

For residents, the absence of cases means none has come to light, not that none exists. They are best protected when they can see who funds officials, who wins public contracts and who owns the companies that do business with the state.

Seychelles.d:
Little has been proven about outsiders reaching into the Seychelles state, and what has been reported centres on the heroin that moves through the islands of the western Indian Ocean. People who use drugs, prison staff and former anti-narcotics officers interviewed for research published in 2021 described police who release dealers after a payment, resell seized drugs and protect some traffickers while pursuing their rivals, and they said corruption in the anti-narcotics bureau reaches high. A parliamentary committee separately found irregular payments of about US$6 million, involving the drug-enforcement agency and the financial intelligence unit, sent to offshore companies in Mauritius.

None of this has been tested in court: as of 2021 the Anti-Corruption Commission had no active case of drug-related corruption. The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 4 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5.4, both near the middle of the scale.

For residents this means the agencies they are told are fighting the drug trade are described as compromised by the people who work closest to them, while no court has yet said who was paid or by whom. In a 2017 survey by the Anti-Corruption Commission, more than four in five of the roughly 15,000 people who answered said corruption was very high.

Slovenia.d:
The documented attempt from outside to buy decisions in Slovenia came through arms buying, the part of government where a single contract is large and the details are kept from the public. In 2006 Patria, a Finnish state-owned arms maker, won a deal worth 278 million euros to supply 135 armoured vehicles, and the Finnish broadcaster YLE later alleged that bribes were paid partly aimed at Prime Minister Janez Janša.

Courts in three countries reached different conclusions. A Slovenian conviction of Janša was annulled by the Constitutional Court and the case lapsed without a new ruling; defendants in Finland were acquitted, and one middleman was convicted in Austria. No court has a standing finding that Janša took money, and he denies it.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 6.5 out of 10, higher than most of its EU neighbours, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 6.2.

For Slovenians, the Patria case shows what that gap looks like in practice. Taxpayers paid for the country's largest arms purchase while a foreign broadcaster said it had been won with bribes, and voters have had to judge the prime minister at several elections since without a final answer from any court.

South Sudan.d:
South Sudan's government has let outsiders into its core through businessmen who live off state contracts and then move into high office. Benjamin Bol Mel, whose construction company received road contracts worth tens of millions of dollars without competitive bidding while he was the president's financial adviser, was sanctioned by the United States for corruption in 2017 and still became a vice president and deputy head of the ruling party in 2025, until a decree removed him nine months later.

Oil is the state's main income, and foreign commodity traders have bought access to it through officials. Glencore admitted in a UK court in 2022 to paying bribes for oil business in five African countries, South Sudan among them.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 9 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at about 2, among the worst in the world. For South Sudanese this means oil revenue that belongs to the public is traded through officials for private payments, and contracts go to people close to the president without a tender.

St. Lucia.d:
Nothing is documented here, so this is an estimate. No case has been found of foreign governments, companies or criminal groups paying or placing officials in St Lucia.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 3 out of 10, which is low, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5.5, near the middle of the scale. The main risk in the eastern Caribbean is the cocaine route north from South America, which passes through these islands.

For residents, the absence of a documented case means there is no known instance of officials here being paid or placed from outside. It also means the estimate rests on the index's own assessment rather than on any investigation or court case in St Lucia, and it would change if a case came to light, most likely through the drug route.

Sweden.d:
In Sweden the reach into the state comes mainly from criminal networks working through ordinary public administration rather than through politicians. A 2023 research review for the SNS think tank found that criminal networks have people inside government agencies, run companies in the welfare sector, such as home care, schools and assistance services, and draw on social insurance; wrong welfare payments are estimated at 13 to 16 billion kronor a year. Municipalities are most exposed, because they spend much of the money with less oversight. Courts have convicted police employees of passing data from police registers to these networks, and police reporting calls insider access a systematic weakness.

An older episode shows how close private power has sat to the state. In the Second World War the government used the heads of the Wallenberg family's bank for its trade talks while the same bank held German-owned companies on paper for the German firm Bosch, which the US treated as hiding enemy property.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 2 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 7.4. For Swedes this shows where the problem lies: their taxes fund welfare companies that criminal groups run, the losses fall on municipal budgets for care and schools, and people who report crimes or give evidence can be identified to the groups they reported from inside the police.

Tajikistan.d:
Tajikistan's long border with Afghanistan is one of the main routes for Afghan heroin and hashish heading north to Russia and Europe, and the drug trade reaches into the officials who are meant to stop it: border guards, police and, at times, diplomats. Analysts and diplomats cited by EurasiaNet in 2012 said some estimate drug money at the equivalent of 30% of the economy, and that major traffickers enjoy high-level protection.

Two cases show how far up it has gone. In 2000 Kazakh security officers seized about 62 kilograms of heroin near Almaty from two cars, one of them the Tajik ambassador's, and arrested him. In 2012 a military court jailed five officers of a border unit in Khatlon province, on the Afghan frontier, after the checkpoint chief was caught with 20 kilograms of hashish.

Convictions stop at that level. No prosecution has reached the people diplomats describe as protecting the trade, and most seizures are of small dealers. The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 9 out of 10, among the highest in the world, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 2.5.

For people in Tajikistan this means the border is a route rather than a barrier, police and prison guards are reported to control street and prison sales, and if drug money makes up a large share of the economy, many families depend on it for work while officials who refuse to go along are at risk.

Togo.d:
Nothing documented yet shows a foreign government, company, crime group or secret society paying officials or placing people inside Togo's government or companies, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions.

The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, puts Togo in its High band, scoring it 7.5 out of 10 on that measure. It gives about 4.4 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, which is below the middle of the range. Read together, those scores suggest that outside interests have room to reach officials and that the bodies which would expose them are weak.

For people living in Togo, the absence of a documented case means none has come to light, not that none exists. Public contracts, the ownership of companies that do business with the state, and who funds political campaigns are the records where it would first show.

Turkiye.d:
Turkey's story of infiltration is mostly told by its own government, which says that for decades the Gülen movement, a religious network led by the preacher Fethullah Gülen, placed its followers as judges, prosecutors, police officers and military officers. The government blames those followers for the failed coup of July 2016 and now treats the movement as a terrorist group under the name 'FETÖ'. About 150,000 people were dismissed from public jobs by emergency decree, without a court ruling on each person, including about a third of the country's judges in a single day.

Courts have convicted hundreds of air force and army officers as the coup's organisers. For most of the people dismissed, though, the evidence of membership was never tested, and the earlier mass trials that the government now blames on Gülen-linked prosecutors were themselves overturned for forged and unlawful evidence.

A second, older pattern links the state to Turkey's ultranationalist street movement, the Grey Wolves, the youth wing of the MHP party that now governs in partnership with President Erdoğan's AKP. In 1996 a car crash at Susurluk killed a deputy Istanbul police chief alongside a Grey Wolves gunman wanted by Interpol, who carried papers signed by the interior minister, and a parliamentary inquiry concluded that state bodies had been using the group. In 2020 a prison-release law freed the crime boss Alaattin Çakıcı, who then publicly thanked the MHP's leader.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Turkey at 9 out of 10. For people in Turkey this means a public servant can lose a career on an accusation of hidden loyalty, judges know their colleagues were removed overnight, and gunmen and gangsters with nationalist ties have repeatedly been found working alongside the police.

Ukraine.d:
Ukraine is fighting a war against Russia while still dealing with networks that reach into its state companies and border posts from inside. The danger shows most clearly where Russian state interests and Ukrainian industry overlap: prosecutors charge that managers of Motor Sich, a maker of helicopter and aircraft engines, kept supplying engines and parts to Russia's state technology corporation Rostec, and its former president is on trial for treason.

The more common pattern is a business circle close to those in power taking a cut from state firms. In 2025 Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau said a group led by Timur Mindich, a businessman and friend of President Zelensky, took about $100 million in kickbacks from contractors of Energoatom, the state nuclear power company; two ministers were asked to resign and a former deputy prime minister was charged. At the western border in Zakarpattia, customs and border officers have been charged with running the smuggling channels into the European Union that they are paid to close.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Ukraine at 8 out of 10, and its courts, police and watchdogs at 4.5. For Ukrainians, kickbacks at the nuclear company raise the cost of keeping electricity on while Russia bombs the grid, and leaks from defence suppliers can reach the army that is shelling them. Smuggling at the western crossings works only as long as the officers there are paid to look away, and the cost of each scheme falls on a public budget already stretched by the war.

Uruguay.d:
Uruguay has strong courts and watchdogs by world standards, and no current case shows outside groups with people inside its government. The Global Organized Crime Index puts it in the Low band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 3.5 out of 10 and the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs at 7.5.

The documented case of outside reach comes from the years of military rule, when a foreign religious movement bought its way into the financial system. In 1981 the Unification Church, the Korean-founded movement of Sun Myung Moon, bought 49% of Banco de Crédito, one of the country's oldest banks, and started a daily newspaper that declared itself 'fully identified' with the military government. A later parliamentary commission found that the bank had lent about US$100 million, about a sixth of all its loans, to companies linked to Moon's movement before it closed in 2002.

The effect is still felt by Uruguayans who kept their savings in that bank or depended on its stability: a foreign group that owned almost half of it used depositors' money to fund its own companies, under a government that faced no free press or opposition able to ask questions. That case is the reason the risk is not zero, but in present-day Uruguay the courts, parliament and press are able to investigate such an arrangement if it happened again.

Venezuela.d:
In Venezuela the state itself has been accused of becoming a channel for drug trafficking. US prosecutors say senior military and political figures have protected cocaine shipments and armed the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla army, and they use the name 'Cartel de los Soles' for this network of officers; analysts dispute that it is an organised cartel. The accused include those in charge of the bodies meant to stop the trade: a head of military intelligence and a retired general have pleaded guilty in US courts, while a head of the anti-drug office charged in New York was promoted to interior minister instead of being removed. Nicolás Maduro, seized by US forces in January 2026, has pleaded not guilty and has not yet been tried.

A second route ran through Cuba. Under secret agreements signed in 2008, Cuban officers oversaw the rebuilding of Venezuela's military intelligence service, which then turned to watching Venezuela's own soldiers. Foreign contractors have also been accused of buying access through campaign payments in return for priority on public works, claims no Venezuelan court has examined.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Venezuela at 9 out of 10 and its courts, police and watchdogs at 1.9, among the lowest in the world. For Venezuelans this has meant police and anti-drug agencies led by men accused of working for traffickers, soldiers who disagreed with the government being watched under foreign supervision, and public works contracts awarded without open scrutiny. There is no domestic court able to examine any of these accusations.

Zimbabwe.d:
In Zimbabwe the line between the ruling party and the businesses that profit from the state has largely disappeared. The pattern is for a small circle of business people close to President Mnangagwa and the ZANU-PF party to win state contracts paid with public money, and then to move into the party and the government themselves. The clearest example is Kudakwashe Tagwirei, whose company Sakunda grew through fuel trading and a $3 billion state farming contract paid in Treasury bills; the United States and Britain sanctioned him for misappropriating public funds, which he denies, and in October 2026 he was made a cabinet minister in charge of investment.

The same overlap runs through the gold trade, Zimbabwe's main source of hard currency. In 2023 undercover reporters recorded brokers, one of them holding the government post of ambassador-at-large, offering to launder cash through the state gold refinery and export it as bullion. The government appointed a commission, and the practice continued.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Zimbabwe at 8 out of 10 and its courts, police and watchdogs at 3. For Zimbabweans this means that money meant for fuel, seed and fertiliser passes through firms owned by people who now sit in the cabinet, and gold dug from their land can be used to clean criminal money abroad. Investment policy is now run by a man two Western governments accuse of taking public funds.
